observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =xy=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+18{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }26{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}26{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-9(2\pi -0) \\  & =-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x=12\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =3y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24{cos}^{2}⁡t+24{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24\,\text{d}t \\  & =24t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =24(2\pi -0) \\  & =48\pi \end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.name: Calculating Flux for Non-Closed Curves
tutorial.problem:
As we've seen, the flux of a vector field $\mathbf F$ through a piecewise-smooth, closed curve $C$ is a unique scalar number that represents the net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ 

The question now is, does the notion of flux exist for curves that are not closed?

Indeed, it is possible to define the notion of flux through a non-closed curve. However, there is one crucial difference we need to bear in mind:

- In the case of a smooth, closed curve, it is always clear which direction is "out." Therefore, the outward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ is unique at every point on $C.$

- However, on a smooth, non-closed curve, there is no clear notion of "in" and "out." Instead, we can choose between *two* normal vectors at any point on the curve, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/d193eb8109ead15de50c06a7bb0b654243173d882bd361f9fd34026aa23c1b5f.png)

Therefore, when computing the flux of a vector field through a non-closed curve, we first specify the direction that the unit normal points and then measure the flux relative to that direction. 

For example, for the vector field $\mathbf F$ and curve $C$ below, one choice for the unit normal will give a positive number, and the other a negative number.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/4f92dd5334b5836703857c081049f126d39c141e84d8e94171e338a162cf3cc4.png)

Finally, to calculate the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across a non-closed curve $C,$ we can continue to use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

**Watch Out!** To apply this formula, we usually need to parameterize $C.$ It is *vital* that we pick a parameterization where the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ is a $90^\circ$ *clockwise* rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
y = \dfrac{t^2}{4},
\qquad
t\in \left[0,4\right].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(4,4).$ Therefore, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/2b94e24344f600fc02ec5ecac6c1e0ee4c6a5450132753a0a5ac5fceaa9aa1fc.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-2, \\ Q(x,y) & =x=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})=\frac{t}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$

question.problem:

The curve $C$ is given by $y = \dfrac14x^2$ from the point $\left(0,0\right)$ to the point $\left(4,4\right).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = -2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
y = \dfrac{t^2}{4},
\qquad
t\in \left[0,4\right].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(4,4).$ Therefore, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/2b94e24344f600fc02ec5ecac6c1e0ee4c6a5450132753a0a5ac5fceaa9aa1fc.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-2, \\ Q(x,y) & =x=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})=\frac{t}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(-2)\cdot (\frac{t}{2})-(t)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-16-0 \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,y=t,\,t\in [\frac{1}{e},1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/08fc4561a322b690da7bd28a9e69a91c687256e8a902ec7690dda5e6a1c689a6.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =0, \\ Q(x,y) & =2{y}^{2}=2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=-\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(0)\cdot (1)-(2{t}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2}){|}_{1/e}^{1} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13

The curve C is given by x=−ln⁡y from the point (1,1e) to the point (0,1). Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=2y2j through C, measured with respect to the unit normal vector n on C, as shown above.

a
1−e2
b
1−1e2
c
0
d
1+e2
e
1+1e2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of F across C measured with respect to a unit normal vector n on C is given by ∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx. To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector T(t).

Parameterizing the curve C, we have x=−ln⁡ty=t,t∈[1e,1].

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point (1,1e) to the point (0,1). Therefore, n is indeed a 90∘ clockwise rotation of T, so we can apply the above formula for the flux.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=0,Q(x,y)=2y2=2t2.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(−ln⁡t)=−1t,dydt=ddt(t)=1.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx=∫1/e1(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫1/e1(0)⋅(1)−(2t2)⋅(−1t)dt=∫1/e12tdt=(t2)|1/e1=1−1e2

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/559bbc20aa7d47eaad47a8975f80c8efb91bd03bc816357bc6047675dc755c9b.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =5{e}^{-x}=5{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\frac{5}{t}, \\ Q(x,y) & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{5}{t})\cdot (1)-(4)\cdot (\frac{1}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t{|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/e90c36e34c6ab51f15707685a22c8bd2c749b9857ca24c59631f09dfbda495c6.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={t}^{2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =y={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t)\cdot (2t)-({t}^{2})\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j$ for $t\in [0,1],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/e90c36e34c6ab51f15707685a22c8bd2c749b9857ca24c59631f09dfbda495c6.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={t}^{2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =y={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t)\cdot (2t)-({t}^{2})\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=xi+yj through the curve C given by r(t)=ti+t2j for t∈[0,1], measured with respect to the unit normal vector n on C, as shown above.

a
1
b
−23
c
43
d
23
e
13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of F across C measured with respect to a unit normal vector n on C is given by ∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx. To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector T(t).

In this case, n is indeed a 90∘ clockwise rotation of T, so we can apply the above formula.

Along the curve C, we have x=t,y=t2.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=x=t,Q(x,y)=y=t2.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(t)=1,dydt=ddt(t2)=2t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx=∫01(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫01(t)⋅(2t)−(t2)⋅(1)dt=∫01t2dt=13t3|01=13

tutorial.name: Deriving the Main Formula
tutorial.problem:
Let's now derive the following formula for the flux:

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_C P\,\textrm{d}y- Q\,\textrm{d}x
$$

First, recall that if $C$ is parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then 

$$
\mathbf n = \dfrac{y'(t)\,\mathbf i - x'(t)\,\mathbf j}{||\mathbf r'(t)||},
$$

where it is assumed that $C$ is positively-oriented. 

Substituting our expression for $\mathbf n$ into our line integral definition of flux and using the fact that $\textrm d s = ||\mathbf r'(t)|| \,\textrm d t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{{y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||})||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{{y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j}{\cancel{||{r}^{′}(t)||}})\cancel{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot ({y}^{′}(t)\,i-{x}^{′}(t)\,j)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}P(x(t),y(t)){y}^{′}(t)-Q(x(t),y(t)){x}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

steps.html:
Calculating Flux for Non-Closed Curves
?

As we've seen, the flux of a vector field through a piecewise-smooth, closed curve is a unique scalar number that represents the net flow of through

The question now is, does the notion of flux exist for curves that are not closed?

Indeed, it is possible to define the notion of flux through a non-closed curve. However, there is one crucial difference we need to bear in mind:

  • In the case of a smooth, closed curve, it is always clear which direction is "out." Therefore, the outward-pointing unit normal vector is unique at every point on

  • However, on a smooth, non-closed curve, there is no clear notion of "in" and "out." Instead, we can choose between two normal vectors at any point on the curve, as shown below.

Therefore, when computing the flux of a vector field through a non-closed curve, we first specify the direction that the unit normal points and then measure the flux relative to that direction.

For example, for the vector field and curve below, one choice for the unit normal will give a positive number, and the other a negative number.

Finally, to calculate the flux of across a non-closed curve we can continue to use the formula

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=xy\,i+{x}^{2}\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=4{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(4{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}-16{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=xyi+x2j across the closed curve C given by r(t)=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj for t∈[0,2π).

a
−16π3
b
0
c
−32π3
d
16π3
e
32π3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

Along the curve C, we have x=2cos⁡t,y=2sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=xy=4sin⁡tcos⁡t,Q(x,y)=x2=4cos2⁡t.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(2cos⁡t)=−2sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(2sin⁡t)=2cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution u=cos⁡t,du=−sin⁡tdt, as follows:

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∫02π(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫02π(4sin⁡tcos⁡t)⋅(2cos⁡t)−(4cos2⁡t)⋅(−2sin⁡t)dt=∫02π8sin⁡tcos2⁡t+8sin⁡tcos2⁡tdt=∫02π16sin⁡tcos2⁡tdt=∫11−16u2du=0

last_observation.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=4{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(4{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}-16{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=xy\,i+{x}^{2}\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=4{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(4{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}-16{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=y\,i+9{x}^{3}\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =9{x}^{3}=9{cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{cos}⁡t=u,du=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(9{cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{1}^{1}(u+{u}^{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=yi+9x3j across the closed curve C given by r(t)=cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj for t∈[0,2π).

c

EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

Along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=y=3sin⁡t,Q(x,y)=9x3=9cos3⁡t.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(cos⁡t)=−sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(3sin⁡t)=3cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution cos⁡t=u,du=−sin⁡tdt, as follows:

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∫02π(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫02π(3sin⁡t)⋅(3cos⁡t)−(9cos3⁡t)⋅(−sin⁡t)dt=9∫02π(sin⁡tcos⁡t+sin⁡tcos3⁡t)dt=−9∫11(u+u3)du=0

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+(y-x)\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x+y=3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t), \\ Q(x,y) & =y-x=3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =9t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =9(2\pi -0) \\  & =18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x+y=3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t), \\ Q(x,y) & =y-x=3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(3(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =9t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =9(2\pi -0) \\  & =18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=(x+y)i+(y−x)j across the closed curve C given by r(t)=3cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj for t∈[0,2π).

a
 18π
b
 −9π
c
 9π
d
 −18π
e
 0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

Along the curve C, we have x=3cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=x+y=3(cos⁡t+sin⁡t),Q(x,y)=y−x=3(sin⁡t−cos⁡t).

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(3cos⁡t)=−3sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(3sin⁡t)=3cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∫02π(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫02π(3(cos⁡t+sin⁡t))⋅(3cos⁡t)−(3(sin⁡t−cos⁡t))⋅(−3sin⁡t)dt=9∫02π(cos2⁡t+sin⁡tcos⁡t+sin2⁡t−sin⁡tcos⁡t)dt=9∫02π1dt=9t|02π=9(2π−0)=18π

solution.reasoning: The divergence is ∂(x+y)/∂x + ∂(y−x)/∂y = 2. Green's flux theorem therefore gives outward flux 2 times the area of the radius-3 disk: 2·9π = 18π, option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different question.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i+j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=49{cos}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(49{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(1)\cdot (-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{3}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-98{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}-98{u}^{2}\,du \\  & =(98\operatorname{sin}⁡t-7\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}

Question 4
?

Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=x2i+j across the closed curve C given by r(t)=7cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj for t∈[0,2π).

a
 −7π
b
 14π
c
 7π
d
 0
e
 −14π
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

Along the curve C, we have x=7cos⁡t,y=2sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=x2=49cos2⁡t,Q(x,y)=1.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(7cos⁡t)=−7sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(2sin⁡t)=2cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution sin⁡t=u,du=cos⁡tdt, as follows:

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∫02π(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫02π(49cos2⁡t)⋅(2cos⁡t)−(1)⋅(−7sin⁡t)dt=∫02π98cos3⁡t+7sin⁡tdt=∫02π98cos2⁡t⋅cos⁡t+7sin⁡tdt=∫02π98(1−sin2⁡t)cos⁡t+7sin⁡tdt=∫02π98(cos⁡t−sin2⁡tcos⁡t)+7sin⁡tdt=∫02π98cos⁡t+7sin⁡tdt+∫02π−98sin2⁡tcos⁡tdt=∫02π98cos⁡t+7sin⁡tdt+∫00−98u2du=(98sin⁡t−7cos⁡t)|02π+0=0

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=49{cos}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(49{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(1)\cdot (-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{3}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-98{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}-98{u}^{2}\,du \\  & =(98\operatorname{sin}⁡t-7\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

solution.reasoning: The divergence is ∂(x²)/∂x + ∂1/∂y = 2x. By Green's flux theorem, the outward flux is the integral of 2x over the enclosed ellipse. question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =30{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =30{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =30(2\pi -0) \\  & =60\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=xi+yj across the closed curve C given by r(t)=5cos⁡ti+6sin⁡tj for t∈[0,2π).

a
0
b
−60π
c
30π
d
60π
e
−30π
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

Along the curve C, we have x=5cos⁡t,y=6sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=x=5cos⁡t,Q(x,y)=y=6sin⁡t.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(5cos⁡t)=−5sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(6sin⁡t)=6cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∫02π(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫02π(5cos⁡t)⋅(6cos⁡t)−(6sin⁡t)⋅(−5sin⁡t)dt=30∫02π(cos2⁡t+sin2⁡t)dt=30∫02π1dt=30(2π−0)=60π

solution.reasoning: The divergence is ∂x/∂x + ∂y/∂y = 2. The enclosed ellipse has area π·5·6 = 30π, so Green's flux theorem gives outward flux 2·30π = 60π, option d. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example answers a different question.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =30{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =30{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =30(2\pi -0) \\  & =60\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(1-x)\,i+(x-y)\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $16{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=144.$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $4,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1-x=1-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x-y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-12{cos}^{2}⁡t+9\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-12{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t-12{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t+9{\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u-12{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0-12t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =4(0-0)-12(2\pi -0) \\  & =-24\pi \end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

First, we write the equation of our curve as

x232+y242=1.

The closed curve C is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 3 and 4, respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

r(t)=3cos⁡ti+4sin⁡tj,0≤t≤2π.

Along the curve C, we have x=3cos⁡t,y=4sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=1−x=1−3cos⁡t,Q(x,y)=x−y=3cos⁡t−4sin⁡t.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(3cos⁡t)=−3sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(4sin⁡t)=4cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution u=sin⁡t,du=cos⁡tdt, as follows:

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=100.$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $5$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={e}^{y}={e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={e}^{x}={e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitutions $u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,du=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt$ and $v=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,dv=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u+{\int }_{1}^{1}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =0\end{aligned}

Question 7
?

Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=eyi+exj across the ellipse C with equation 4x2+25y2=100.

a
e2(1−e3)
b
−e3
c
0
d
2e2(1−e3)
e
e3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

First, we write the equation of our curve as

x252+y222=1.

The closed curve C is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 5 and 2, respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

r(t)=5cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj,0≤t≤2π.

Along the curve C, we have x=5cos⁡t,y=2sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=ey=e2sin⁡t,Q(x,y)=ex=e5cos⁡t.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(5cos⁡t)=−5sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(2sin⁡t)=2cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitutions u=2sin⁡t,du=2cos⁡tdt and v=5cos⁡t,dv=−5sin⁡tdt, as follows:

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∫02π(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫02π(e2sin⁡t)⋅(2cos⁡t)−(e5cos⁡t)⋅(−5sin⁡t)dt=∫02π(e2sin⁡t)⋅(2cos⁡t)dt−∫02π(e5cos⁡t)⋅(−5sin⁡t)dt=∫00eudu+∫11evdv=0

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $5$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={e}^{y}={e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={e}^{x}={e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitutions $u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,du=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt$ and $v=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,dv=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u+{\int }_{1}^{1}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=100.$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $5$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={e}^{y}={e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={e}^{x}={e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitutions $u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,du=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt$ and $v=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,dv=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u+{\int }_{1}^{1}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i+xy\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=36.$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =xy=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+18{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }26{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}26{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $3$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}=4{sin}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =xy=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+18{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }26{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}26{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

First, we write the equation of our curve as

x232+y222=1.

The closed curve C is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 3 and 2, respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

r(t)=3cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj,0≤t≤2π.

Along the curve C, we have x=3cos⁡t,y=2sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=y2=4sin2⁡t,Q(x,y)=xy=6sin⁡tcos⁡t.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(3cos⁡t)=−3sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(2sin⁡t)=2cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution u=sin⁡t,du=cos⁡tdt, as follows:

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∫02π(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫02π(4sin2⁡t)⋅(2cos⁡t)−(6sin⁡tcos⁡t)⋅(−3sin⁡t)dt=∫02π8sin2⁡tcos⁡t+18sin2⁡tcos⁡tdt=∫02π26sin2⁡tcos⁡tdt=∫1126u2du=0

solution.reasoning: The divergence is ∂(y²)/∂x + ∂(xy)/∂y = x. By Green's flux theorem, the outward flux is the integral of x over the enclosed ellipse. Symmetry about the y-axis makes this integral zero, so option c is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different question.

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(y-x)\,i-(x+y)\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={3}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-9(2\pi -0) \\  & =-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=(y−x)i−(x+y)j across the circle C with equation x2+y2=9

a
0
b
−18π
c
9π
d
−9π
e
18π
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

First, we write the equation of our curve as

x2+y2=32.

The closed curve C is a circle centered at the origin with the radius 1. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

r(t)=3cos⁡ti+3sin⁡tj,0≤t≤2π.

Along the curve C, we have x=3cos⁡t,y=3sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=y−x=3sin⁡t−3cos⁡t,Q(x,y)=−(x+y)=−3cos⁡t−3sin⁡t.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(3cos⁡t)=−3sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(3sin⁡t)=3cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∫02π(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫02π(3sin⁡t−3cos⁡t)⋅(3cos⁡t)−(−3cos⁡t−3sin⁡t)⋅(−3sin⁡t)dt=9∫02π(sin⁡tcos⁡t−cos2⁡t−sin⁡tcos⁡t−sin2⁡t)dt=9∫02π−(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)dt=−9∫02πdt=−9t|02π=−9(2π−0)=−18π

solution.reasoning: The divergence is ∂(y−x)/∂x + ∂(−x−y)/∂y = −2. The circle encloses area 9π, so Green's flux theorem gives outward flux −2·9π = −18π, option b. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked example concerns a different question.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(y-x)\,i-(x+y)\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={3}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-9(2\pi -0) \\  & =-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=3x\,i+3y\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64.$
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x=12\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =3y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24{cos}^{2}⁡t+24{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24\,\text{d}t \\  & =24t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =24(2\pi -0) \\  & =48\pi \end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 10
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x=12\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =3y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24{cos}^{2}⁡t+24{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24\,\text{d}t \\  & =24t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =24(2\pi -0) \\  & =48\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

First, we write the equation of our curve as

x242+y222=1.

The closed curve C is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes 4 and 2, respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

r(t)=4cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj,0≤t≤2π.

Along the curve C, we have x=4cos⁡t,y=2sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=3x=12cos⁡t,Q(x,y)=3y=6sin⁡t.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(4cos⁡t)=−4sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(2sin⁡t)=2cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∫02π(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫02π(12cos⁡t)⋅(2cos⁡t)−(6sin⁡t)⋅(−4sin⁡t)dt=∫02π24cos2⁡t+24sin2⁡tdt=∫02π24dt=24t|02π=24(2π−0)=48π

solution.reasoning: The ellipse is x²/16 + y²/4 = 1, so its area is π·4·2 = 8π. The divergence is ∂(3x)/∂x + ∂(3y)/∂y = 6. Green's flux theorem gives outward flux 6·8π = 48π, option d. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different question.

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/cd21413d8eea5e2fec67eebe22967c846fd7916fd4fb0fbe5f8efe7ac9df6b1a.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $y=1-x$ from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,0).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=\,i+\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=1-t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,0).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/e288ed1095be61e4645fb63c22b7fd2cb605d34795c30557e84afb31b7ec8721.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1)\cdot (-1)-(1)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-2t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-2-0 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 11
?

The curve C is given by y=1−x from the point (0,1) to the point (1,0). Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=i+j through C, measured with respect to the unit normal vector n on C, as shown above.

a
1
b
−2
c
−1
d
2
e
0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of F across C measured with respect to a unit normal vector n on C is given by ∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx. To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector T(t).

Parameterizing the curve C, we have x=t,y=1−t,t∈[0,1].

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point (0,1) to the point (1,0). Therefore, n is indeed a 90∘ clockwise rotation of T, so we can apply the above formula for the flux.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=1,Q(x,y)=1.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(t)=1,dydt=ddt(1−t)=−1.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx=∫01(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫01(1)⋅(−1)−(1)⋅(1)dt=∫01−2dt=(−2t)|01=−2−0=−2

last_observation.name: Question 11
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=1-t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,0).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/e288ed1095be61e4645fb63c22b7fd2cb605d34795c30557e84afb31b7ec8721.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1)\cdot (-1)-(1)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-2t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-2-0 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of F across C measured with respect to a unit normal vector n on C is given by ∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx. To apply this formula,

  • the unit normal vector n must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector T(t).

Therefore,

P(x,y)=y2=t2,Q(x,y)=1x=e−t.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(et)=et,dydt=ddt(t)=1.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx=∫01(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫01(t2)⋅(1)−(e−t)⋅(et)dt=∫01t2−1dt=(t33−t)|01=(13−1)−0=−23

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/62c8f6d7db345ce76bd164bb52c13e5edef9c04f18f4f07501c8694e7f64b554.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $x={e}^{y}$ from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
feedback.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={e}^{t}\,y=t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/ba6285008fd90835fdbf73203b76a0a01d713889d9939979aaec54bebd0a8c49.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x}={e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2})\cdot (1)-({e}^{-t})\cdot ({e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
