question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/67dca8f0202d0c5d1041935a6aee7c4ebd0e3c6c449f2ee1a5ff24c1f381410c.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2{y}^{2}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,y=t,\,t\in [\frac{1}{e},1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/08fc4561a322b690da7bd28a9e69a91c687256e8a902ec7690dda5e6a1c689a6.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =0, \\ Q(x,y) & =2{y}^{2}=2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=-\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(0)\cdot (1)-(2{t}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2}){|}_{1/e}^{1} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 13
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,y=t,\,t\in [\frac{1}{e},1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,\frac{1}{e})$ to the point $(0,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/08fc4561a322b690da7bd28a9e69a91c687256e8a902ec7690dda5e6a1c689a6.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =0, \\ Q(x,y) & =2{y}^{2}=2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=-\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}(0)\cdot (1)-(2{t}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/e}^{1}2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2}){|}_{1/e}^{1} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

The curve C is given by x=−ln⁡y from the point (1,1e) to the point (0,1). Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=2y2j through C, measured with respect to the unit normal vector n on C, as shown above.

a
1−e2
b
1−1e2
c
0
d
1+e2
e
1+1e2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of F across C measured with respect to a unit normal vector n on C is given by ∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx. To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector T(t).

Parameterizing the curve C, we have x=−ln⁡ty=t,t∈[1e,1].

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point (1,1e) to the point (0,1). Therefore, n is indeed a 90∘ clockwise rotation of T, so we can apply the above formula for the flux.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=0,Q(x,y)=2y2=2t2.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(−ln⁡t)=−1t,dydt=ddt(t)=1.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx=∫1/e1(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫1/e1(0)⋅(1)−(2t2)⋅(−1t)dt=∫1/e12tdt=(t2)|1/e1=1−1e2

solution.reasoning: Parameterize C by r(t)=(−ln t,t), with 1/e≤t≤1. The pictured northeast normal is the clockwise normal, so n ds=(1,1/t)dt. Therefore the flux is ∫[1/e,1] 2t²(1/t)dt = [t²][1/e,1] = 1−1/e², option b. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different question.

Question 13
?

The curve C is given by x=−ln⁡y from the point (1,1e) to the point (0,1). Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=2y2j through C, measured with respect to the unit normal vector n on C, as shown above.

a
1−e2
b
1−1e2
c
0
d
1+e2
e
1+1e2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of F across C measured with respect to a unit normal vector n on C is given by ∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx. To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector T(t).

Parameterizing the curve C, we have x=−ln⁡ty=t,t∈[1e,1].

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point (1,1e) to the point (0,1). Therefore, n is indeed a 90∘ clockwise rotation of T, so we can apply the above formula for the flux.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=0,Q(x,y)=2y2=2t2.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(−ln⁡t)=−1t,dydt=ddt(t)=1.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx=∫1/e1(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫1/e1(0)⋅(1)−(2t2)⋅(−1t)dt=∫1/e12tdt=(t2)|1/e1=1−1e2

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/85b4da8c0fa35867871b6254ba20f505b7596f2c97226adb2ed01339fe4cbedf.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=5{e}^{-x}\,i+4\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,e],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/559bbc20aa7d47eaad47a8975f80c8efb91bd03bc816357bc6047675dc755c9b.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =5{e}^{-x}=5{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\frac{5}{t}, \\ Q(x,y) & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{5}{t})\cdot (1)-(4)\cdot (\frac{1}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t{|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=5e−xi+4j through the curve C given by r(t)=ln⁡ti+tj for t∈[1,e], measured with respect to the unit normal vector n on C, as shown above.

a
 0
b
 −1
c
 1
d
 2
e
 −2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of F across C measured with respect to a unit normal vector n on C is given by ∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx. To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector T(t).

In this case, n is indeed a 90∘ clockwise rotation of T, so we can apply the above formula.

Along the curve C, we have x=ln⁡t,y=t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=5e−x=5e−ln⁡t=5t,Q(x,y)=4.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(ln⁡t)=1t,dydt=ddt(t)=1.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx=∫1e(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫1e(5t)⋅(1)−(4)⋅(1t)dt=∫1e1tdt=ln⁡t|1e=1
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve

solution.reasoning: The pictured southeast normal is the clockwise normal to r′(t)=(1/t,1), so n ds=(1,−1/t)dt. Along C, F=(5/t,4). Hence the flux is ∫₁ᵉ(5/t−4/t)dt = [ln t]₁ᵉ = 1, option c. feedback.name: Question 14
feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/85b4da8c0fa35867871b6254ba20f505b7596f2c97226adb2ed01339fe4cbedf.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=5{e}^{-x}\,i+4\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡t\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,e],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
feedback.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/559bbc20aa7d47eaad47a8975f80c8efb91bd03bc816357bc6047675dc755c9b.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =5{e}^{-x}=5{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\frac{5}{t}, \\ Q(x,y) & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)=\frac{1}{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{5}{t})\cdot (1)-(4)\cdot (\frac{1}{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡t{|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/c71395cfe5877546509f24656ba23f0883cbd3ee8c145c10abae9600c8bd5c4a.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j$ for $t\in [0,1],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/e90c36e34c6ab51f15707685a22c8bd2c749b9857ca24c59631f09dfbda495c6.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={t}^{2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =y={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t)\cdot (2t)-({t}^{2})\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve
last_observation.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224381/assets/e90c36e34c6ab51f15707685a22c8bd2c749b9857ca24c59631f09dfbda495c6.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y={t}^{2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =y={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t)\cdot (2t)-({t}^{2})\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=xi+yj through the curve C given by r(t)=ti+t2j for t∈[0,1], measured with respect to the unit normal vector n on C, as shown above.

a
1
b
−23
c
43
d
23
e
13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of F across C measured with respect to a unit normal vector n on C is given by ∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx. To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector T(t).

In this case, n is indeed a 90∘ clockwise rotation of T, so we can apply the above formula.

Along the curve C, we have x=t,y=t2.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=x=t,Q(x,y)=y=t2.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(t)=1,dydt=ddt(t2)=2t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx=∫01(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫01(t)⋅(2t)−(t2)⋅(1)dt=∫01t2dt=13t3|01=13

Consider two sets of $25$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{25},$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{25}.$ You are given that

$$
\begin{aligned} & {\sum }_{i=1}^{25}{x}_{i}=250, \\  & {\sum }_{i=1}^{25}{y}_{i}=265, \\  & {\sum }_{i=1}^{25}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}=3\,625.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, ${S}_{xy}=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ the statistic ${S}_{xy}$ be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}-\frac{1}{n}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given statistics in the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & =3\,625-\frac{1}{25}(250)(265) \\  & =3\,625-2\,650 \\  & =975.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ the sum of squared deviations from the mean for the data ${x}_{i}$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-\frac{1}{n}{({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given statistics in the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & =12\,050-\frac{1}{27}(540)^{2} \\  & =12\,050-10\,800 \\  & =1\,250.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider two sets of $39$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{39},$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{39}.$ You are given that

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx}=663,\,{S}_{yy}=1\,092,\,{S}_{xy}=975.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, $Cov(x,y)=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ their covariance can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Cov(x,y) & =\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${S}_{xy}$ is the sum of products of the deviations of ${x}_{i}$ and ${y}_{i}$ from their means.

We are given that ${S}_{xy}=975.$ Substituting the given statistic in the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Cov(x,y) & =\frac{975}{39} \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we calculate the sum of the ${x}_{i}$ data:

$$

$$

Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ their covariance can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Cov(x,y) & =\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${S}_{xy}$ is the sum of products of the deviations of ${x}_{i}$ and ${y}_{i}$ from their means.

We are given that ${S}_{xy}=975.$ Substituting the given statistic in the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Cov(x,y) & =\frac{975}{39} \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ the sum of squared deviations from the mean for the data ${x}_{i}$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-\frac{1}{n}{({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we calculate the sum of the ${x}_{i}$ data:

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{7}{x}_{i}=12+\,14+\,9+\,17+\,15+\,10+\,14=91.
$$

We are given that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{7}{x}_{i}^{2}=1\,231.$

Finally, by substituting into the above formula, we get

$$
{S}_{xx}=1\,231-\frac{1}{7}(91)^{2}=1231-1\,183=48.

question.worked_solution:
Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ the statistic ${S}_{xy}$ be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}{y}_{i}-\frac{1}{n}({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given statistics in the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & =3\,625-\frac{1}{25}(250)(265) \\  & =3\,625-2\,650 \\  & =975.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}Cov(x,y) & =\frac{975}{39} \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ the sum of squared deviations from the mean for the data ${x}_{i}$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}^{2}-\frac{1}{n}{({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we calculate the sum of the ${x}_{i}$ data:

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{7}{x}_{i}=12+\,14+\,9+\,17+\,15+\,10+\,14=91.
$$

We are given that ${\sum }_{i=1}^{7}{x}_{i}^{2}=1\,231.$

Finally, by substituting into the above formula, we get

$$
{S}_{xx}=1\,231-\frac{1}{7}(91)^{2}=1231-1\,183=48.
$$

xi 12 14 9 1715 10 14
yi 15 18 11 10 20 15 16

Given that ∑i=17xi2=1231, calculate Sxx.

a
Sxx=48
b
Sxx=119
c
Sxx=26
d
Sxx=122
e
Sxx=87.2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate the sum of the xi data: ∑i=17xi=12+14+9+17+15+10+14=91.

We are given that ∑i=17xi2=1231.

Finally, by substituting into the above formula, we get Sxx=1231−17(91)2=1231−1183=48.

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the two sets of 7 paired observations shown in the table below.


xi 12 14 9 1715 10 14
yi 15 18 11 10 20 15 16

Given that ∑i=17xi2=1231, calculate Sxx.

a
Sxx=48
b
Sxx=119
c
Sxx=26
d
Sxx=122
e
Sxx=87.2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Given a set of n paired observations x1,x2,…,xn and y1,y2,…,yn, the sum of squared deviations from the mean for the data xi can be calculated as follows: Sxx=∑i=1n(xi−x―)2=∑i=1nxi2−1n(∑i=1nxi)2.

First, we calculate the sum of the xi data: ∑i=17xi=12+14+9+17+15+10+14=91.

We are given that ∑i=17xi2=1231.

Finally, by substituting into the above formula, we get Sxx=1231−17(91)2=1231−1183=48.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/182a88f3f8f379dd35228cbb6ebe5c34d9761608a6a222710f50d8f272d3cf1e.png)

Calculate $\operatorname{cos}⁡R.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡R=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{QR}{PR}=\frac{2}{PR}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $PR.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}PR & =\sqrt{P{Q}^{2}+Q{R}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{5})^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5+4} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡R & =\frac{2}{PR}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: In a right triangle $△LMN,$ $∠M$ is a right angle, $MN=\sqrt{5}$ and $LM=\sqrt{11}.$ Determine the cosine of $∠N.$
questions.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/df7dcd343dd2676cb38b7df3c2d8cb599fed45b9c0b25194609effe2bf27a6f7.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡N=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{MN}{LN}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{LN}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $LN.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}LN & =\sqrt{M{N}^{2}+L{M}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{5})^{2}+(\sqrt{11})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5+11} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡N & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{LN}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/e585e89d11dea316c5483eeb2b2fc4750084409651ecf838e65a0d09e7bcc97f.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡G=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{GH}{FG}=\frac{GH}{6}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $GH.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}GH & =\sqrt{F{G}^{2}-F{H}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}-(2\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36-8} \\  & =\sqrt{28} \\  & =2\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡G & =\frac{GH}{6} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{7}}{6} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: In a right triangle $△XYZ,$ $∠X$ is a right angle, $XZ=\sqrt{5}$ and $YZ=7.$ Find the cosine of $∠Y.$
questions.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/ea0502e8b261358c7b55c60df02474c5b39a75cbb104d6ba3efb40300294ef56.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡Y=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{XY}{YZ}=\frac{XY}{7}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $XY.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{Y{Z}^{2}-X{Z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{7}^{2}-(\sqrt{5})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{49-5} \\  & =\sqrt{44} \\  & =2\sqrt{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡Y & =\frac{XY}{7}=\frac{2\sqrt{11}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/de81dfe9ea7efd41a7ca5b576452c62491ab438dbb0b75eb7c7a6c13a903fe6f.png)

Determine the cosine of $∠Q.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡Q=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{QR}{PQ}=\frac{QR}{8.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $QR.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{Q}^{2}-P{R}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(8.5)^{2}-(7.5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{72.25-56.25} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡Q & =\frac{QR}{8.5} \\  & =\frac{4}{8.5} \\  & =\frac{40}{85} \\  & =\frac{8}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/bdc0ea077dce75d6de1250ee6cf2e6dbd119b5124330c9a92edc071e475d0755.png)

Find the sine of $∠U.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of sine: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡U=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{ST}{SU}=\frac{ST}{12.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $ST.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}ST & =\sqrt{S{U}^{2}-T{U}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(12.5)^{2}-(7.5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{156.25-56.25} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡U & =\frac{ST}{12.5} \\  & =\frac{10}{12.5} \\  & =\frac{100}{125} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: In a right triangle $△OMN,$ $∠M$ is a right angle, $MN=1.8$ and $ON=3.$ Determine $\operatorname{cos}⁡O.$
questions.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/5c980bff90a516627618909a863b4919dbb10be1b674911cae663f3f7c54f3fb.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡O=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{OM}{ON}=\frac{OM}{3}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $OM.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}OM & =\sqrt{O{N}^{2}-M{N}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}-{1.8}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9-3.24} \\  & =\sqrt{5.76} \\  & =2.4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡O & =\frac{OM}{3} \\  & =\frac{2.4}{3} \\  & =\frac{24}{30} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the tangent of $∠N.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of tangent: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡N=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{OM}{MN}=\frac{OM}{2.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $OM.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}OM & =\sqrt{O{N}^{2}-M{N}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{6.5}^{2}-{2.5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{42.25-6.25} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡N & =\frac{OM}{2.5} \\  & =\frac{6}{2.5} \\  & =\frac{60}{25} \\  & =\frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Evaluating a Trigonometric Ratio by Using the Pythagorean Theorem to Solve for the Hypotenuse
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the value of $\cos L.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/78416d3c8ec8a8351ecfe0a4ea81feb05cce29f55dd9ec4bc676e6363dd49ec0.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\cos L = \dfrac {\textrm{adjacent}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac {JL}{KL} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{KL}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $KL.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\eqalign{
KL &= \sqrt{ JK^2 + JL^2 } \
&= \sqrt{ (3)^2 + (3\sqrt3)^2 } \
&= \sqrt{  9 + 27 } \
&= \sqrt{36}\
&= 6\
	}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
	\cos L &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{KL} \[5pt] 
&= \dfrac{3\sqrt 3}{6} \[5pt] 
&=\dfrac {\sqrt 3} 2.
}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the sine of $\angle Y.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/e0fb47c85d56c314389a0a334029b3b769f13ddcca6ab15a9021cf6361e4b1ce.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of sine: 

$$
\sin Y = \dfrac {\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac {XZ}{YZ} = \dfrac{XZ}{61}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $XZ.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\eqalign{
XZ &= \sqrt{ YZ^2 - XY^2 } \
&= \sqrt{ 61^2 - 60^2 } \
&= \sqrt{ 3721- 3600 } \
&= \sqrt{121 }\
&= 11
	}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
		\sin Y&= \dfrac{XZ}{61} = \dfrac{11}{61}.
	}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate $\tan K.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/fbac8700b860cbe8a60f2c24a5ab7ee9e7adfda584b1077edf208b0dcd16744e.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of tangent: 

$$
\tan K = \dfrac {\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{adjacent}} = \dfrac {JL}{JK} = \dfrac{JL}{7.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $JL.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\eqalign{
JL &= \sqrt{ KL^2 - JK^2 } \
&= \sqrt{ 12.5^2 - 7.5^2 } \
&= \sqrt{ 156.25-56.25 } \
&= \sqrt{100 }\
&= 10
	}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
		\tan K&= \dfrac{JL}{7.5}\[5pt]
 &= \dfrac{10}{7.5}  \[5pt]
 &=\dfrac 4 3.
	}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we have a right triangle $\triangle ABC$ with legs $AC= BC = 1,$ like the one in the diagram below.
How can we find the value $\sin \theta$ if we don't know one of the relevant sides?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/ae5157e6824fd98861194302ab912e76d9e79dade6706dfbedea97d859f18a79.png)

Recall the definition of sine: 

$$
\sin \theta = \dfrac {\textrm{opposite}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac {AC}{AB} = \dfrac 1 c
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $c.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\sqrt{A{C}^{2}+B{C}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can finish computing the value of $\sin\theta\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1\cdot \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

No matter which trigonometric function we need to find, if we are missing one of the relevant sides but we know the lengths of the other two sides, we can always use the Pythagorean Theorem.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\cos L = \dfrac {\textrm{adjacent}}{\textrm{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac {JL}{KL} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{KL}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $KL.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\eqalign{
KL &= \sqrt{ JK^2 + JL^2 } \
&= \sqrt{ (3)^2 + (3\sqrt3)^2 } \
&= \sqrt{  9 + 27 } \
&= \sqrt{36}\
&= 6\
	}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
	\cos L &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{KL} \[5pt] 
&= \dfrac{3\sqrt 3}{6} \[5pt] 
&=\dfrac {\sqrt 3} 2.
}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡R=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{QR}{PR}=\frac{2}{PR}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $PR.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}PR & =\sqrt{P{Q}^{2}+Q{R}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{5})^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5+4} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡R & =\frac{2}{PR}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/182a88f3f8f379dd35228cbb6ebe5c34d9761608a6a222710f50d8f272d3cf1e.png)

Calculate $\operatorname{cos}⁡R.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡R=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{QR}{PR}=\frac{2}{PR}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $PR.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}PR & =\sqrt{P{Q}^{2}+Q{R}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{5})^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5+4} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡R & =\frac{2}{PR}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡R=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{QR}{PR}=\frac{2}{PR}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $PR.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}PR & =\sqrt{P{Q}^{2}+Q{R}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{5})^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5+4} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡R & =\frac{2}{PR}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: In a right triangle $△LMN,$ $∠M$ is a right angle, $MN=\sqrt{5}$ and $LM=\sqrt{11}.$ Determine the cosine of $∠N.$
question.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/df7dcd343dd2676cb38b7df3c2d8cb599fed45b9c0b25194609effe2bf27a6f7.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡N=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{MN}{LN}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{LN}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $LN.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}LN & =\sqrt{M{N}^{2}+L{M}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{5})^{2}+(\sqrt{11})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5+11} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡N & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{LN}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

In a right triangle △LMN, ∠M is a right angle, MN=5 and LM=11. Determine the cosine of ∠N.

a
14
b
25
c
114
d
54
e
34
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The following triangle illustrates the information given.

Recall the definition of cosine: cos⁡N=adjacenthypotenuse=MNLN=5LN

Here, we need to determine the missing length LN. The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem: LN=MN2+LM2=(5)2+(11)2=5+11=16=4

Therefore,

cos⁡N=5LN=54.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: In a right triangle $△FGH,$ $∠H$ is a right angle, $FH=2\sqrt{2}$ and $FG=6.$ Find the cosine of $∠G.$
question.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/e585e89d11dea316c5483eeb2b2fc4750084409651ecf838e65a0d09e7bcc97f.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡G=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{GH}{FG}=\frac{GH}{6}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $GH.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}GH & =\sqrt{F{G}^{2}-F{H}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}-(2\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36-8} \\  & =\sqrt{28} \\  & =2\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡G & =\frac{GH}{6} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{7}}{6} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The following triangle illustrates the information given.

Recall the definition of cosine: cos⁡G=adjacenthypotenuse=GHFG=GH6

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem: In a right triangle $△FGH,$ $∠H$ is a right angle, $FH=2\sqrt{2}$ and $FG=6.$ Find the cosine of $∠G.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/e585e89d11dea316c5483eeb2b2fc4750084409651ecf838e65a0d09e7bcc97f.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡G=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{GH}{FG}=\frac{GH}{6}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $GH.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}GH & =\sqrt{F{G}^{2}-F{H}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}-(2\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36-8} \\  & =\sqrt{28} \\  & =2\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡G & =\frac{GH}{6} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{7}}{6} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: In a right triangle $△XYZ,$ $∠X$ is a right angle, $XZ=\sqrt{5}$ and $YZ=7.$ Find the cosine of $∠Y.$
question.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/ea0502e8b261358c7b55c60df02474c5b39a75cbb104d6ba3efb40300294ef56.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡Y=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{XY}{YZ}=\frac{XY}{7}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $XY.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}XY & =\sqrt{Y{Z}^{2}-X{Z}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{7}^{2}-(\sqrt{5})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{49-5} \\  & =\sqrt{44} \\  & =2\sqrt{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡Y & =\frac{XY}{7}=\frac{2\sqrt{11}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

In a right triangle △XYZ, ∠X is a right angle, XZ=5 and YZ=7. Find the cosine of ∠Y.

a
257
b
4117
c
2117
d
57
e
227
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The following triangle illustrates the information given.

Recall the definition of cosine: cos⁡Y=adjacenthypotenuse=XYYZ=XY7

Here, we need to determine the missing side XY. The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem: XY=YZ2−XZ2=72−(5)2=49−5=44=211

Therefore,

cos⁡Y=XY7=2117.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/de81dfe9ea7efd41a7ca5b576452c62491ab438dbb0b75eb7c7a6c13a903fe6f.png)

Determine the cosine of $∠Q.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡Q=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{QR}{PQ}=\frac{QR}{8.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $QR.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{Q}^{2}-P{R}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(8.5)^{2}-(7.5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{72.25-56.25} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡Q & =\frac{QR}{8.5} \\  & =\frac{4}{8.5} \\  & =\frac{40}{85} \\  & =\frac{8}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the sine of $∠U.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of sine: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡U=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{ST}{SU}=\frac{ST}{12.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $ST.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}ST & =\sqrt{S{U}^{2}-T{U}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(12.5)^{2}-(7.5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{156.25-56.25} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡U & =\frac{ST}{12.5} \\  & =\frac{10}{12.5} \\  & =\frac{100}{125} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of sine: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡U=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{ST}{SU}=\frac{ST}{12.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing length $ST.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}ST & =\sqrt{S{U}^{2}-T{U}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(12.5)^{2}-(7.5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{156.25-56.25} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡U & =\frac{ST}{12.5} \\  & =\frac{10}{12.5} \\  & =\frac{100}{125} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall the definition of sine: sin⁡U=oppositehypotenuse=STSU=ST12.5

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: In a right triangle $△OMN,$ $∠M$ is a right angle, $MN=1.8$ and $ON=3.$ Determine $\operatorname{cos}⁡O.$
question.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/5c980bff90a516627618909a863b4919dbb10be1b674911cae663f3f7c54f3fb.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡O=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{OM}{ON}=\frac{OM}{3}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $OM.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}OM & =\sqrt{O{N}^{2}-M{N}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}-{1.8}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9-3.24} \\  & =\sqrt{5.76} \\  & =2.4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡O & =\frac{OM}{3} \\  & =\frac{2.4}{3} \\  & =\frac{24}{30} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

In a right triangle △OMN, ∠M is a right angle, MN=1.8 and ON=3. Determine cos⁡O.

a
34
b
45
c
25
d
 14
e
35
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The following triangle illustrates the information given.

Recall the definition of cosine: cos⁡O=adjacenthypotenuse=OMON=OM3

Here, we need to determine the missing side OM. The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem: OM=ON2−MN2=32−1.82=9−3.24=5.76=2.4

Therefore,

cos⁡O=OM3=2.43=2430=45.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The following triangle illustrates the information given.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/5c980bff90a516627618909a863b4919dbb10be1b674911cae663f3f7c54f3fb.png)

Recall the definition of cosine: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡O=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{OM}{ON}=\frac{OM}{3}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $OM.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}OM & =\sqrt{O{N}^{2}-M{N}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}-{1.8}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9-3.24} \\  & =\sqrt{5.76} \\  & =2.4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡O & =\frac{OM}{3} \\  & =\frac{2.4}{3} \\  & =\frac{24}{30} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

In a right triangle △OMN, ∠M is a right angle, MN=1.8 and ON=3. Determine cos⁡O.

a
34
b
45
c
25
d
 14
e
35
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The following triangle illustrates the information given.

Recall the definition of cosine: cos⁡O=adjacenthypotenuse=OMON=OM3

Here, we need to determine the missing side OM. The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem: OM=ON2−MN2=32−1.82=9−3.24=5.76=2.4

Therefore,

cos⁡O=OM3=2.43=2430=45.

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/f9f59d4328ad43e6e342da3cf9e87ccd5dfe33b97c46424e7fcc2b9f562fc452.png)

Find the tangent of $∠N.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of tangent: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡N=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{OM}{MN}=\frac{OM}{2.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $OM.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}OM & =\sqrt{O{N}^{2}-M{N}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{6.5}^{2}-{2.5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{42.25-6.25} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡N & =\frac{OM}{2.5} \\  & =\frac{6}{2.5} \\  & =\frac{60}{25} \\  & =\frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

a
512
b
1213
c
1312
d
 513
e
125
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the definition of tangent: tan⁡N=oppositeadjacent=OMMN=OM2.5

Here, we need to determine the missing side OM. The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem: OM=ON2−MN2=6.52−2.52=42.25−6.25=36=6

Therefore,

tan⁡N=OM2.5=62.5=6025=125.

question.html:
Question 8
?

Find the tangent of ∠N.

a
512
b
1213
c
1312
d
 513
e
125
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the definition of tangent: tan⁡N=oppositeadjacent=OMMN=OM2.5

Here, we need to determine the missing side OM. The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem: OM=ON2−MN2=6.52−2.52=42.25−6.25=36=6

Therefore,

tan⁡N=OM2.5=62.5=6025=125.
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Trigonometric Ratio by Using the Pythagorean Theorem with Decimals

solution.reasoning: The right angle is at M, so NO is the hypotenuse. MO = \sqrt{6.5^2-2.5^2} = \sqrt{36} = 6. Thus \tan N = MO/MN = 6/2.5 = 12/5, option e. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224552/assets/f9f59d4328ad43e6e342da3cf9e87ccd5dfe33b97c46424e7fcc2b9f562fc452.png)

Find the tangent of $∠N.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall the definition of tangent: 

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡N=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{OM}{MN}=\frac{OM}{2.5}
$$

Here, we need to determine the missing side $OM.$ The trick is to use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}OM & =\sqrt{O{N}^{2}-M{N}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{6.5}^{2}-{2.5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{42.25-6.25} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡N & =\frac{OM}{2.5} \\  & =\frac{6}{2.5} \\  & =\frac{60}{25} \\  & =\frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=16.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $4$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=\frac{1}{9}.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\frac{1}{3}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \frac{1}{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1/3}{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2$ for $y\le 0.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14224175/assets/6f35be4fd6773149597ea8a9dc8dd234e068da3f0fd3b2df32d11c61521bed75.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{2},\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & ={\rho }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=16$ for $x\le 0.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}2x({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $4$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14224175/assets/8c803dbf5bcf6c2ece6c1c8352f96da1c88734ca1d792dd05593ac8c11527b2b.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=2x({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ((\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}) \\  & =2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ({\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) \\  & =2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ({\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )) \\  & =2\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ({\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ) \\  & =2{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2x({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}2{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4}2{\rho }^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{4}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=5.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}(x+z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\sqrt{5}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{5},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=(x+z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(x+z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Sphere
questions.raw_html:
5.Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Sphere?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=5. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭R(x+z)x2+y2+z2dV

E
Wed, Oct 14th @ 10:28 PM|Elapsed: 0:14Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $4$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=16. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Ryx2+y2+z2dV

a
∫0π∫02π∫04ρ4cos⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
∫0π∫02π∫016ρ3sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
∫0π∫02π∫04ρ4sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
∫02π∫02π∫016ρ3cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
∫02π∫02π∫04ρ4cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents the sphere of radius 4 centered at the origin. As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤4,0≤θ≤2π,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=yx2+y2+z2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ=ρ2sin⁡θsin⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\frac{1}{3}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \frac{1}{3},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}+{(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1/3}{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=19. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Ryzx2+y2dV

a
∫0π∫02π∫01/3ρ2sin⁡θcos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
∫02π∫02π∫01/3ρ3sin2⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
∫0π∫02π∫01/9ρ3sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
∫02π∫02π∫03ρ2sin2⁡ϕcos2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
∫0π∫02π∫01/9ρ2cos⁡θcos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents the sphere of radius 13 centered at the origin. As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤13,0≤θ≤2π,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=yzx2+y2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ⋅ρcos⁡ϕ(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2+(ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2=ρ2sin⁡θsin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕρ2sin2⁡ϕ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=sin⁡θcos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕ

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14224175/assets/6f35be4fd6773149597ea8a9dc8dd234e068da3f0fd3b2df32d11c61521bed75.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{2},\,\pi \le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ+{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ} \\  & ={\rho }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=2 for y≤0. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Rzx2+y2dV

a
 ∫0π∫π2π∫02ρ4cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
∫0π∫π2π∫02ρ4cos⁡ϕsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
 ∫0π∫0π∫02ρ4cos⁡ϕsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
 ∫0π∫0π∫02ρ2sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
∫0π∫π/23π/2∫02ρ2sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents one-half of the sphere of radius 2 centered at the origin.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤2,π≤θ≤2π,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=zx2+y2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=ρcos⁡ϕ(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2+(ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2=ρcos⁡ϕρ2cos2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ+ρ2sin2⁡θsin2⁡ϕ=ρcos⁡ϕρ2sin2⁡ϕ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=ρcos⁡ϕρ2sin2⁡ϕ=ρ2cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭Rzx2+y2dV=∭Δρ2cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫π2π∫02ρ4cos⁡ϕsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $4$ centered at the origin.

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2x({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}2{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4}2{\rho }^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{4}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\sqrt{5}$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le \sqrt{5},\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=(x+z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}(x+z)\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{5}}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ+\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=5. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭R(x+z)x2+y2+z2dV

a
∫0π∫02π∫05ρ4sin⁡ϕ(cos⁡θsin⁡ϕ+cos⁡ϕ)dρdθdϕ
b
∫02π∫02π∫05ρ3sin⁡ϕ(cos2⁡θ+cos⁡ϕ)dρdθdϕ
c
∫0π∫02π∫05ρ3sin⁡ϕcos⁡θ(sin⁡ϕ+1)dρdθdϕ
d
∫02π∫02π∫05ρ4sin⁡ϕ(cos⁡θsin⁡ϕ+sin⁡θcos⁡ϕ)dρdθdϕ
e
∫0π∫02π∫05ρ4(sin⁡ϕ+cos⁡θ)dρdθdϕ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents the sphere of radius 5 centered at the origin. As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤5,0≤θ≤2π,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=(x+z)x2+y2+z2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ+ρcos⁡ϕ)⋅ρ=ρ2(cos⁡θsin⁡ϕ+cos⁡ϕ)

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭R(x+z)x2+y2+z2dV=∭Δρ2(cos⁡θsin⁡ϕ+cos⁡ϕ)⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫02π∫05ρ4sin⁡ϕ(cos⁡θsin⁡ϕ+cos⁡ϕ)dρdθdϕ.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=16.$
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$
question.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $4$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=16. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Ryx2+y2+z2dV

a
∫0π∫02π∫04ρ4cos⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
∫0π∫02π∫016ρ3sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
∫0π∫02π∫04ρ4sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
∫02π∫02π∫016ρ3cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
∫02π∫02π∫04ρ4cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents the sphere of radius 4 centered at the origin. As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤4,0≤θ≤2π,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=yx2+y2+z2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ=ρ2sin⁡θsin⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭Ryx2+y2+z2dV=∭Δρ2sin⁡θsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫02π∫04ρ4sin⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $4$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi \}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot \rho  \\  & ={\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}{\rho }^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
