last_observation.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We're given that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-u-v,\,v-u,\,2⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨x,\,y,\,-z⟩|}_{x=u+v\,y=v-u\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨u+v,\,v-u,\,-uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u+v,\,v-u,\,-uv⟩\cdot ⟨-u-v,\,v-u,\,2⟩ \\  & =(u+v)\cdot (-u-v)+(v-u)\cdot (v-u)+(-uv)\cdot 2 \\  & =-{u}^{2}-2uv-{v}^{2}+{v}^{2}-2uv+{u}^{2}-2uv \\  & =-6uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨x,\,y,\,-z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-6uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{0}uv\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-6{\int }_{0}^{1}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{-2}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-6\cdot [\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =-6\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot (-2) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨-x-z,\,x-y,\,-z⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,v-u,\,-v⟩
$$

for $-1\le u\le 0$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨-x-z,\,x-y,\,-z⟩|}_{x=u+v\,y=v-u\,z=-v} \\  & =⟨-(u+v)-(-v),\,u+v-(v-u),\,-(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-u,\,2u,\,v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨-u,\,2u,\,v⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,1,\,2⟩ \\  & =(-u)\cdot 1+2u\cdot 1+v\cdot 2 \\  & =-u+2u+2v \\  & =u+2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x-z,\,x-y,\,-z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(u+2v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}(u+2v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[uv+{v}^{2}]_{v=0}^{v=1}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(u+1)\text{d}u \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}+u]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

for $-1\le u\le 0$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨-x-z,\,x-y,\,-z⟩|}_{x=u+v\,y=v-u\,z=-v} \\  & =⟨-(u+v)-(-v),\,u+v-(v-u),\,-(-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨-u,\,2u,\,v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨-u,\,2u,\,v⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,1,\,2⟩ \\  & =(-u)\cdot 1+2u\cdot 1+v\cdot 2 \\  & =-u+2u+2v \\  & =u+2v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨-x-z,\,x-y,\,-z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(u+2v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}(u+2v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[uv+{v}^{2}]_{v=0}^{v=1}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(u+1)\text{d}u \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}+u]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨2x,\,\frac{xz}{3}-2y,\,2z⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u-1,\,uv,\,3v⟩
$$

over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 2\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨3v,\,-6,\,2u⟩.$*
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We're given that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨3v,\,-6,\,2u⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨2x,\,\frac{xz}{3}-2y,\,2z⟩|}_{x=2u-1\,y=uv\,z=3v} \\  & =⟨2(2u-1),\,\frac{(2u-1)(3v)}{3}-2uv,\,2(3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨4u-2,\,-v,\,6v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨4u-2,\,-v,\,6v⟩\cdot ⟨3v,\,-6,\,2u⟩ \\  & =(4u-2)\cdot 3v+(-v)\cdot (-6)+6v\cdot 2u \\  & =12uv-6v+6v+12uv \\  & =24uv.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨2x,\,\frac{xz}{3}-2y,\,2z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}24uv\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}24uv\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}[12{u}^{2}v]_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}12v\,\text{d}v \\  & =[6{v}^{2}]_{-1}^{2} \\  & =6({2}^{2}-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨3v,\,-6,\,2u⟩.

question.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨3,\,z,\,y⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
r(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2},\,v,\,uv⟩
$$

for $-1\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2u & 0 & v \\ 0 & 1 & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & v \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|,-|\begin{aligned}2u & v \\ 0 & u\end{aligned}|,|\begin{aligned}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-v,\,-2{u}^{2},\,2u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨3,\,z,\,y⟩|}_{x={u}^{2}\,y=v\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨3,\,uv,\,v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3,\,uv,\,v⟩\cdot ⟨-v,\,-2{u}^{2},\,2u⟩ \\  & =3\cdot (-v)+uv\cdot (-2{u}^{2})+v\cdot 2u \\  & =-3v-2{u}^{3}v+2uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨3,\,z,\,y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-3v-2{u}^{3}v+2uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-3v-2{u}^{3}v+2uv)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-3uv-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{4}v+{u}^{2}v]}_{u=-1}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-6v)\text{d}v \\  & =[-3{v}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Evaluate the surface integral ∬S⟨3,z,y⟩⋅dS

where the parametric surface S is defined by the equations

r(u,v)=⟨u2,v,uv⟩

for −1≤u≤1 and 0≤v≤1.

a
−3
b
−1
c
4
d
52
e
−12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the flux of a vector field F over S is given by ∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬DF(r(u,v))⋅(ru′×rv′)dA.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves: ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(u2),∂∂u(v),∂∂u(uv)⟩=⟨2u,0,v⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(u2),∂∂v(v),∂∂v(uv)⟩=⟨0,1,u⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is

ru′×rv′=|ijk2u0v01u|=⟨|0v10|,−|2uv0u|,|2u001|⟩=⟨−v,−2u2,2u⟩.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into F(x,y,z): F(r(u,v))=⟨3,z,y⟩|x=u2y=vz=uv=⟨3,uv,v⟩

Finally, we calculate the dot product of F and ru′×rv′: F(r(u,v))⋅(ru′×rv′)=⟨3,uv,v⟩⋅⟨−v,−2u2,2u⟩=3⋅(−v)+uv⋅(−2u2)+v⋅2u=−3v−2u3v+2uv

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to ∬S⟨3,z,y⟩⋅dS=∬DF(r(u,v))⋅(ru′×rv′)dA=∬D(−3v−2u3v+2uv)dA=∫01∫−11(−3v−2u3v+2uv)dudv=∫01[−3uv−12u4v+u2v]u=−1u=1dv=∫01(−6v)dv=[−3v2]01=−3.

solution.reasoning: The tangent vectors are r_u=⟨2u,0,v⟩ and r_v=⟨0,1,u⟩, so r_u×r_v=⟨−v,−2u²,2u⟩. Substituting gives F(r(u,v))=⟨3,uv,v⟩, hence the integrand is −3v−2u³v+2uv. The odd terms in u integrate to zero over [−1,1], leaving −3·2·(1/2)=−3, option a. No Math Academy key or grade for this question is captured; the worked solution concerns a different example.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨3,\,z,\,y⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
r(u,v)=⟨{u}^{2},\,v,\,uv⟩
$$

for $-1\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨2u,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2u & 0 & v \\ 0 & 1 & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & v \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|,-|\begin{aligned}2u & v \\ 0 & u\end{aligned}|,|\begin{aligned}2u & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-v,\,-2{u}^{2},\,2u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨3,\,z,\,y⟩|}_{x={u}^{2}\,y=v\,z=uv} \\  & =⟨3,\,uv,\,v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3,\,uv,\,v⟩\cdot ⟨-v,\,-2{u}^{2},\,2u⟩ \\  & =3\cdot (-v)+uv\cdot (-2{u}^{2})+v\cdot 2u \\  & =-3v-2{u}^{3}v+2uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨3,\,z,\,y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-3v-2{u}^{3}v+2uv)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-3v-2{u}^{3}v+2uv)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-3uv-\frac{1}{2}{u}^{4}v+{u}^{2}v]}_{u=-1}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-6v)\text{d}v \\  & =[-3{v}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨3z,\,-2x,\,-y⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
r(u,v)=⟨-v,\,-u,\,{u}^{2}⟩
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-1,\,2u⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -1 & 2u \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2u \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,-|\begin{aligned}0 & 2u \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|,|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2u,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨3z,\,-2x,\,-y⟩|}_{x=-v\,y=-u\,z={u}^{2}} \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,-2(-v),\,-(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,2v,\,u⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-2u,\,-1⟩ \\  & =3{u}^{2}\cdot 0+2v\cdot (-2u)+u\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4uv-u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨3z,\,-2x,\,-y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4uv-u)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4uv-u)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4uv+u)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{u}^{2}v+\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{u=0}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}(2v+\frac{1}{2})\text{d}v \\  & =-{[{v}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}v]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Evaluate the surface integral ∬S⟨3z,−2x,−y⟩⋅dS

where the parametric surface S is defined by the equations

r(u,v)=⟨−v,−u,u2⟩

for 0≤u≤1 and 0≤v≤1.

a
−18
b
−13
c
−14
d
−32
e
13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the flux of a vector field F over S is given by ∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬DF(r(u,v))⋅(ru′×rv′)dA.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves: ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(−v),∂∂u(−u),∂∂u(u2)⟩=⟨0,−1,2u⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(−v),∂∂v(−u),∂∂v(u2)⟩=⟨−1,0,0⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is

ru′×rv′=|ijk0−12u−100|=⟨|−12u00|,−|02u−10|,|0−1−10|⟩=⟨0,−2u,−1⟩.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into F(x,y,z): F(r(u,v))=⟨3z,−2x,−y⟩|x=−vy=−uz=u2=⟨3u2,−2(−v),−(−u)⟩=⟨3u2,2v,u⟩

Then, we calculate the dot product of F and ru′×rv′: F(r(u,v))⋅(ru′×rv′)=⟨3u2,2v,u⟩⋅⟨0,−2u,−1⟩=3u2⋅0+2v⋅(−2u)+u⋅(−1)=−4uv−u

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to ∬S⟨3z,−2x,−y⟩⋅dS=∬DF(r(u,v))⋅(ru′×rv′)dA=∬D(−4uv−u)dA=∫01∫01(−4uv−u)dudv=−∫01∫01(4uv+u)dudv=−∫01[2u2v+12u2]u=0u=1dv=−∫01(2v+12)dv=−[v2+12v]01=−32.

last_observation.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-1,\,2u⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -1 & 2u \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2u \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,-|\begin{aligned}0 & 2u \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|,|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2u,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨3z,\,-2x,\,-y⟩|}_{x=-v\,y=-u\,z={u}^{2}} \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,-2(-v),\,-(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,2v,\,u⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-2u,\,-1⟩ \\  & =3{u}^{2}\cdot 0+2v\cdot (-2u)+u\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4uv-u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨3z,\,-2x,\,-y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4uv-u)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4uv-u)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4uv+u)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{u}^{2}v+\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{u=0}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}(2v+\frac{1}{2})\text{d}v \\  & =-{[{v}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}v]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Evaluate the surface integral ∬S⟨3z,−2x,−y⟩⋅dS

where the parametric surface S is defined by the equations

r(u,v)=⟨−v,−u,u2⟩

for 0≤u≤1 and 0≤v≤1.

a
−18
b
−13
c
−14
d
−32
e
13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the flux of a vector field F over S is given by ∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬DF(r(u,v))⋅(ru′×rv′)dA.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves: ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(−v),∂∂u(−u),∂∂u(u2)⟩=⟨0,−1,2u⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(−v),∂∂v(−u),∂∂v(u2)⟩=⟨−1,0,0⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is

ru′×rv′=|ijk0−12u−100|=⟨|−12u00|,−|02u−10|,|0−1−10|⟩=⟨0,−2u,−1⟩.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into F(x,y,z): F(r(u,v))=⟨3z,−2x,−y⟩|x=−vy=−uz=u2=⟨3u2,−2(−v),−(−u)⟩=⟨3u2,2v,u⟩

Then, we calculate the dot product of F and ru′×rv′: F(r(u,v))⋅(ru′×rv′)=⟨3u2,2v,u⟩⋅⟨0,−2u,−1⟩=3u2⋅0+2v⋅(−2u)+u⋅(−1)=−4uv−u

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to ∬S⟨3z,−2x,−y⟩⋅dS=∬DF(r(u,v))⋅(ru′×rv′)dA=∬D(−4uv−u)dA=∫01∫01(−4uv−u)dudv=−∫01∫01(4uv+u)dudv=−∫01[2u2v+12u2]u=0u=1dv=−∫01(2v+12)dv=−[v2+12v]01=−32.

feedback.name: Question 10
feedback.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨3z,\,-2x,\,-y⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
r(u,v)=⟨-v,\,-u,\,{u}^{2}⟩
$$

for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-1,\,2u⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -1 & 2u \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2u \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,-|\begin{aligned}0 & 2u \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|,|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2u,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & ={⟨3z,\,-2x,\,-y⟩|}_{x=-v\,y=-u\,z={u}^{2}} \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,-2(-v),\,-(-u)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,2v,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,2v,\,u⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-2u,\,-1⟩ \\  & =3{u}^{2}\cdot 0+2v\cdot (-2u)+u\cdot (-1) \\  & =-4uv-u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral evaluates to

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨3z,\,-2x,\,-y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4uv-u)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4uv-u)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4uv+u)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{u}^{2}v+\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{u=0}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}(2v+\frac{1}{2})\text{d}v \\  & =-{[{v}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}v]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Let $F(x)={x}^{2}-2x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ),$ and let $f(x)$ be the **odd** extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,0)?$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{2}-2(-x)) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Let $F(x)=-3x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{6}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,12),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,12), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-12,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-12,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{2}-6(-x)) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+6x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-4) & =-(-4)^{2}-6(-4)=8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Let $F(x)=-3x+2$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x+2$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-3x+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-3x+2\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[(-3x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{3}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }(((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))+\frac{3}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2+\frac{3}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)(-1)^{n}-2)=\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2).
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Let $F(x)={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+8$ for $x\in [0,\pi ),$ and let $f(x)$ be the **odd** extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,0)?$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{3}-2(-x)^{2}+8) \\  & =-(-{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+8) \\  & ={x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Understanding the Odd Extension of a Function
questions.raw_html:
5.Understanding the Odd Extension of a Function?

Let F(x)=x3−2x2+8 for x∈[0,π), and let f(x) be the odd extension of F(x) to x∈(−π,π). What is f(x) for x∈(−π,0)?

E
Wed, Oct 14th @ 10:33 PM|Elapsed: 0:13Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{2}-2(-x)) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Let F(x)=x2−2x for x∈[0,π), and let f(x) be the odd extension of F(x) to x∈(−π,π). What is f(x) for x∈(−π,0)?

a
|x|2+2|x|
b
−x2+2x
c
|−x2+2x|
d
x2−2x
e
−x2−2x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If F(x) is defined on x∈[0,π), the odd extension of F is the function f such that f(x)={F(x),x∈[0,π),−F(−x),x∈(−π,0).

In our case, for x∈(−π,0), we get f(x)=−F(−x)=−((−x)2−2(−x))=−(x2+2x)=−x2−2x.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{6}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

Question 2

Let F(x)=−3x for x∈[0,π). Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the odd 2π-periodic extension f(x) of the function F(x) below.
6(−1)nn
6(1−(−1)n)πn
6(−1)nn
3(−1)nn
3(1−(−1)n)πn
sin⁡(nx)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(nx)
sin⁡(πx)
cos⁡(πx)
f(x)∼∑n=1∞{(6(1−(−1)n)πn)(S0)}⋅{(sin⁡(nx))(S1)}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by bn=2π∫0πf(x)sin⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=−3x for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get bn=−6π∫0πxsin⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=x⇒u′=1v′=sin⁡(nx)⇒v=−1ncos⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain bn=−6π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=−6π(−1n[xcos⁡(nx)]0π+1n∫0πcos⁡(nx)dx)=6nπ((π⋅cos⁡(nπ)−0⋅cos⁡(0))−1n[sin⁡(nx)]0π)=6nπ(πcos⁡(nπ)−1n(sin⁡(nπ)−sin⁡(0)))=6cos⁡(nπ)n.

Therefore, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have bn=6(−1)nn.

Finally, the Fourier sine series is f(x)∼∑n=1∞6(−1)nn⋅sin⁡(nx).

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,12),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,12), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-12,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-12,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{2}-6(-x)) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+6x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-4) & =-(-4)^{2}-6(-4)=8.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x+2$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-3x+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-3x+2\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[(-3x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{3}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }(((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))+\frac{3}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2+\frac{3}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)(-1)^{n}-2)=\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2).
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

Question 4
?
Let F(x)=−3x+2 for x∈[0,π). Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the odd 2π-periodic extension f(x) of the function F(x) below.
2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)
3(1−(−1)n)πn
2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)
3nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)
2nπ((−1)n(3π+2)−2)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(nx)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(πx)
sin⁡(πx)
f(x)∼∑n=1∞{(3(1−(−1)n)πn)(S0)}⋅{(cos⁡(nx))(S1)}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by bn=2π∫0πf(x)sin⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=−3x+2 for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get bn=2π∫0π(−3x+2)sin⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=−3x+2⇒u′=−3v′=sin⁡(nx)⇒v=−1ncos⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain bn=2π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=2π(−1n[(−3x+2)cos⁡(nx)]0π−3n∫0πcos⁡(nx)dx)=−2nπ(((−3π+2)cos⁡(nπ)−2cos⁡(0))+3n[sin⁡(nx)]0π)=−2nπ((−3π+2)cos⁡(nπ)−2+3n(sin⁡(nπ)−sin⁡(0)))=−2nπ((−3π+2)cos⁡(nπ)−2).

Therefore, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have bn=−2nπ((−3π+2)(−1)n−2)=2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2).

Finally, the Fourier sine series is f(x)∼∑n=1∞2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)⋅sin⁡(nx).

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{3}-2(-x)^{2}+8) \\  & =-(-{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+8) \\  & ={x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-8.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Let $F(x)={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+8$ for $x\in [0,\pi ),$ and let $f(x)$ be the **odd** extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,0)?$
question.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{3}-2(-x)^{2}+8) \\  & =-(-{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+8) \\  & ={x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-8.\end{aligned}
$$

Let F(x)=x3−2x2+8 for x∈[0,π), and let f(x) be the odd extension of F(x) to x∈(−π,π). What is f(x) for x∈(−π,0)?

a
|x|3+2|x|2
b
x3+2x2−8
c
−x3−2x2+8
d
x3−2x2+8
e
|−x3−2x2|
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F(x) is defined on x∈[0,π), the odd extension of F is the function f such that f(x)={F(x),x∈[0,π),−F(−x),x∈(−π,0).

In our case, for x∈(−π,0), we get f(x)=−F(−x)=−((−x)3−2(−x)2+8)=−(−x3−2x2+8)=x3+2x2−8.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Let $F(x)={x}^{2}-2x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ),$ and let $f(x)$ be the **odd** extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,0)?$
question.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$

Let F(x)=x2−2x for x∈[0,π), and let f(x) be the odd extension of F(x) to x∈(−π,π). What is f(x) for x∈(−π,0)?

a
|x|2+2|x|
b
−x2+2x
c
|−x2+2x|
d
x2−2x
e
−x2−2x
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

If F(x) is defined on x∈[0,π), the odd extension of F is the function f such that f(x)={F(x),x∈[0,π),−F(−x),x∈(−π,0).

In our case, for x∈(−π,0), we get f(x)=−F(−x)=−((−x)2−2(−x))=−(x2+2x)=−x2−2x.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Let $F(x)={x}^{2}-2x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ),$ and let $f(x)$ be the **odd** extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,0)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{2}-2(-x)) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Let $F(x)=-3x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
question.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{6}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

Question 2
?
Let F(x)=−3x for x∈[0,π). Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the odd 2π-periodic extension f(x) of the function F(x) below.
6(−1)nn
6(1−(−1)n)πn
6(−1)nn
3(−1)nn
3(1−(−1)n)πn
sin⁡(nx)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(nx)
sin⁡(πx)
cos⁡(πx)
f(x)∼∑n=1∞{(6(1−(−1)n)πn)(S0)}⋅{(sin⁡(nx))(S1)}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by bn=2π∫0πf(x)sin⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=−3x for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get bn=−6π∫0πxsin⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=x⇒u′=1v′=sin⁡(nx)⇒v=−1ncos⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain bn=−6π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=−6π(−1n[xcos⁡(nx)]0π+1n∫0πcos⁡(nx)dx)=6nπ((π⋅cos⁡(nπ)−0⋅cos⁡(0))−1n[sin⁡(nx)]0π)=6nπ(πcos⁡(nπ)−1n(sin⁡(nπ)−sin⁡(0)))=6cos⁡(nπ)n.

Therefore, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have bn=6(−1)nn.

Finally, the Fourier sine series is f(x)∼∑n=1∞6(−1)nn⋅sin⁡(nx).

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{6}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

Let F(x)=−3x for x∈[0,π). Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the odd 2π-periodic extension f(x) of the function F(x) below.
6(−1)nn
6(1−(−1)n)πn
6(−1)nn
3(−1)nn
3(1−(−1)n)πn
sin⁡(nx)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(nx)
sin⁡(πx)
cos⁡(πx)
f(x)∼∑n=1∞{(6(1−(−1)n)πn)(S0)}⋅{(sin⁡(nx))(S1)}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by bn=2π∫0πf(x)sin⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=−3x for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get bn=−6π∫0πxsin⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=x⇒u′=1v′=sin⁡(nx)⇒v=−1ncos⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain bn=−6π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=−6π(−1n[xcos⁡(nx)]0π+1n∫0πcos⁡(nx)dx)=6nπ((π⋅cos⁡(nπ)−0⋅cos⁡(0))−1n[sin⁡(nx)]0π)=6nπ(πcos⁡(nπ)−1n(sin⁡(nπ)−sin⁡(0)))=6cos⁡(nπ)n.

Therefore, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have bn=6(−1)nn.

Finally, the Fourier sine series is f(x)∼∑n=1∞6(−1)nn⋅sin⁡(nx).

feedback.problem:
Let $F(x)=-3x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{6}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{6}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{6\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6(-1)^{n}}{n}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).

question.name: Question 3
question.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,12),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,12), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-12,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-12,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{2}-6(-x)) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+6x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-4) & =-(-4)^{2}-6(-4)=8.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Let $F(x)=-3x+2$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
question.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x+2$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-3x+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-3x+2\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[(-3x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{3}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }(((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))+\frac{3}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2+\frac{3}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)(-1)^{n}-2)=\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2).
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

Question 4
?
Let F(x)=−3x+2 for x∈[0,π). Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the odd 2π-periodic extension f(x) of the function F(x) below.
2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)
3(1−(−1)n)πn
2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)
3nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)
2nπ((−1)n(3π+2)−2)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(nx)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(πx)
sin⁡(πx)
f(x)∼∑n=1∞{(3(1−(−1)n)πn)(S0)}⋅{(cos⁡(nx))(S1)}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by bn=2π∫0πf(x)sin⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=−3x+2 for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get bn=2π∫0π(−3x+2)sin⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=−3x+2⇒u′=−3v′=sin⁡(nx)⇒v=−1ncos⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain bn=2π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=2π(−1n[(−3x+2)cos⁡(nx)]0π−3n∫0πcos⁡(nx)dx)=−2nπ(((−3π+2)cos⁡(nπ)−2cos⁡(0))+3n[sin⁡(nx)]0π)=−2nπ((−3π+2)cos⁡(nπ)−2+3n(sin⁡(nπ)−sin⁡(0)))=−2nπ((−3π+2)cos⁡(nπ)−2).

Therefore, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have bn=−2nπ((−3π+2)(−1)n−2)=2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2).

Finally, the Fourier sine series is f(x)∼∑n=1∞2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)⋅sin⁡(nx).

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x+2$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-3x+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-3x+2\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[(-3x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{3}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }(((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))+\frac{3}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2+\frac{3}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)(-1)^{n}-2)=\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2).
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)
3(1−(−1)n)πn
2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)
3nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)
2nπ((−1)n(3π+2)−2)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(nx)
sin⁡(nx)
cos⁡(πx)
sin⁡(πx)
f(x)∼∑n=1∞{(3(1−(−1)n)πn)(S0)}⋅{(cos⁡(nx))(S1)}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by bn=2π∫0πf(x)sin⁡(nx)dx.

In our case, f(x)=−3x+2 for x∈(0,π). So, substituting into the formula, we get bn=2π∫0π(−3x+2)sin⁡(nx)dx.

We use the integration by parts: u=−3x+2⇒u′=−3v′=sin⁡(nx)⇒v=−1ncos⁡(nx)

Thus, we obtain bn=2π(uv|0π−∫0πvu′dx)=2π(−1n[(−3x+2)cos⁡(nx)]0π−3n∫0πcos⁡(nx)dx)=−2nπ(((−3π+2)cos⁡(nπ)−2cos⁡(0))+3n[sin⁡(nx)]0π)=−2nπ((−3π+2)cos⁡(nπ)−2+3n(sin⁡(nπ)−sin⁡(0)))=−2nπ((−3π+2)cos⁡(nπ)−2).

Therefore, since cos⁡(nπ)=(−1)n, we have bn=−2nπ((−3π+2)(−1)n−2)=2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2).

Finally, the Fourier sine series is f(x)∼∑n=1∞2nπ((−1)n(3π−2)+2)⋅sin⁡(nx).

feedback.problem:
Let $F(x)=-3x+2$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot {{field-2}}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-3x+2$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-3x+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-3x+2\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-3 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[(-3x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{3}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }(((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))+\frac{3}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2+\frac{3}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-3\pi +2)(-1)^{n}-2)=\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2).
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(3\pi -2)+2)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(nx).
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Let $F(x)={x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+8$ for $x\in [0,\pi ),$ and let $f(x)$ be the **odd** extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,0)?$
question.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-((-x)^{3}-2(-x)^{2}+8) \\  & =-(-{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+8) \\  & ={x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}-8.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Let F(x)=x3−2x2+8 for x∈[0,π), and let f(x) be the odd extension of F(x) to x∈(−π,π). What is f(x) for x∈(−π,0)?

a
|x|3+2|x|2
b
x3+2x2−8
c
−x3−2x2+8
d
x3−2x2+8
e
|−x3−2x2|
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F(x) is defined on x∈[0,π), the odd extension of F is the function f such that f(x)={F(x),x∈[0,π),−F(−x),x∈(−π,0).

In our case, for x∈(−π,0), we get f(x)=−F(−x)=−((−x)3−2(−x)2+8)=−(−x3−2x2+8)=x3+2x2−8.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Let F(x)=x3−2x2+8 for x∈[0,π), and let f(x) be the odd extension of F(x) to x∈(−π,π). What is f(x) for x∈(−π,0)?

a
|x|3+2|x|2
b
x3+2x2−8
c
−x3−2x2+8
d
x3−2x2+8
e
|−x3−2x2|
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F(x) is defined on x∈[0,π), the odd extension of F is the function f such that f(x)={F(x),x∈[0,π),−F(−x),x∈(−π,0).

In our case, for x∈(−π,0), we get f(x)=−F(−x)=−((−x)3−2(−x)2+8)=−(−x3−2x2+8)=x3+2x2−8.

solution.reasoning: For x<0, oddness gives f(x)=-F(-x)=-[-x^3-2x^2+8]=x^3+2x^2-8, matching option b. Strict oddness also requires resetting f(0)=0 because F(0)=8; this does not affect the requested negative interval. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

Let F(x)=x3−2x2+8 for x∈[0,π), and let f(x) be the odd extension of F(x) to x∈(−π,π). What is f(x) for x∈(−π,0)?

a
|x|3+2|x|2
b
x3+2x2−8
c
−x3−2x2+8
d
x3−2x2+8
e
|−x3−2x2|
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If F(x) is defined on x∈[0,π), the odd extension of F is the function f such that f(x)={F(x),x∈[0,π),−F(−x),x∈(−π,0).

In our case, for x∈(−π,0), we get f(x)=−F(−x)=−((−x)3−2(−x)2+8)=−(−x3−2x2+8)=x3+2x2−8.

$\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that $cot$ is the reciprocal of $tan.$ So first we need to compute tangent:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{PR}{QR}=\frac{3}{QR}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the length $QR,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{Q}^{2}-P{R}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3\sqrt{5})^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{45-9} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{-1}=2.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratios Given a Triangle
canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\csc\theta,$ $\sec\theta,$ and $\cot\theta$ for the triangle below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224584/assets/343917ea041d51cac38619f3577765eee7fbc3ea85e175148b6c591e11ae230b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We compute the three reciprocal trigonometric ratios as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\csc\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac 5 3, \[5pt]
		\sec\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} =  \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac 5 4, \[5pt]
		\cot\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta} = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac 4 3.
	}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratios Given a Triangle

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating a Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratio Given a Triangle Using the Pythagorean Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\sec L$ for $\triangle KLJ$ (shown below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224584/assets/c08613b38502628d71ffa0cdac65400420fb25926a64b747b925ee06d6d560ca.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Remember that $\sec$ is the reciprocal of $\cos.$ So first we need to compute cosine:

$$
\cos L = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JL}{KL} = \dfrac{JL}{5}
$$

To find the length $JL,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}JL & =\sqrt{K{L}^{2}-J{K}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25-9} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\cos L = \dfrac{JL}{5} = \dfrac{4}{5},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡L & ={(\frac{4}{5})}^{-1}=\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The reciprocals of sine, cosine, and tangent are given special names:

- The reciprocal of **sine** is **cosecant**, abbreviated $\csc.$

$$
\csc(\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\sin(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{hypotenuse}}} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}}
$$

- The reciprocal of **cosine** is **secant**, abbreviated $\sec.$

$$
\sec (\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\cos(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{hypotenuse}}} = \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}}
$$

- The reciprocal of **tangent** is **cotangent**, abbreviated $\cot.$

$$
\cot (\theta) = \dfrac 1 {\tan(\theta)} = \dfrac 1 {\dfrac {\text{opposite}} {\text{adjacent}}} = \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}}
$$

Let's write down expressions for $\csc(B),$ $\sec(B),$ and $\cot(B)$ for the triangle below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224584/assets/e98dcc332739ff381e8dc43160a907e471062c5b8a75567ba7dbb8687c008efa.png)

$$
\eqalign{
		\csc(B) &= \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac c b \[5pt]
		\sec(B) &= \dfrac {\text{hypotenuse}} {\text{adjacent}} = \dfrac c a \[5pt]
		\cot(B) &= \dfrac {\text{adjacent}} {\text{opposite}} = \dfrac a b \
	}
$$

tutorials.name: The Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratios and the Pythagorean Theorem
tutorials.problem:
If we are given two sides of a right triangle, how can we calculate the reciprocal ratios $\sec,$ $\csc,$ or $\cot$ when we are missing one of the necessary sides in the ratio?

The trick here is the same that we use for finding $\sin,$ $\cos,$ or $\tan\mathbin{:}$ we use the Pythagorean theorem for finding the missing side.

To illustrate, let's calculate $\csc L$  in the triangle below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224584/assets/9f2e4ea4922783c84a6cb59c5e1532b726d46c9a837a5b1eaa203bbdc6cc1741.png)

Remember that $\csc$ is the reciprocal of $\sin.$ So first we need to compute sine:

$$
\sin L = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JK}{KL} = \dfrac{JK}{4}
$$

To find the length $JK,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}JK & =\sqrt{K{L}^{2}-J{L}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16-9} \\  & =\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\sin L = \dfrac{JK}{4} = \dfrac{ \sqrt{7} }{4},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡L & ={(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot \sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7}\cdot \sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{7}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

\sin L = \dfrac{JK}{4} = \dfrac{ \sqrt{7} }{4},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡L & ={(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot \sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7}\cdot \sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{7}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

The reciprocals of sine, cosine, and tangent are given special names:

tutorial.name: The Reciprocal Trigonometric Ratios and the Pythagorean Theorem
tutorial.problem:
If we are given two sides of a right triangle, how can we calculate the reciprocal ratios $\sec,$ $\csc,$ or $\cot$ when we are missing one of the necessary sides in the ratio?

The trick here is the same that we use for finding $\sin,$ $\cos,$ or $\tan\mathbin{:}$ we use the Pythagorean theorem for finding the missing side.

To illustrate, let's calculate $\csc L$  in the triangle below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224584/assets/9f2e4ea4922783c84a6cb59c5e1532b726d46c9a837a5b1eaa203bbdc6cc1741.png)

Remember that $\csc$ is the reciprocal of $\sin.$ So first we need to compute sine:

$$
\sin L = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \dfrac{JK}{KL} = \dfrac{JK}{4}
$$

To find the length $JK,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}JK & =\sqrt{K{L}^{2}-J{L}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16-9} \\  & =\sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\sin L = \dfrac{JK}{4} = \dfrac{ \sqrt{7} }{4},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{csc}⁡L & ={(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4})}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot \sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{7}\cdot \sqrt{7}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{7}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{PR}{QR}=\frac{3}{QR}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the length $QR,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{Q}^{2}-P{R}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3\sqrt{5})^{2}-{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{45-9} \\  & =\sqrt{36} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{-1}=2.
$$

$$

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡P=\frac{QR}{15}=\frac{12}{15}=\frac{4}{5},
$$

and therefore

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡P={(\frac{4}{5})}^{-1}=\frac{5}{4}.

b

c

d

Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that csc is the reciprocal of sin. So first we need to compute sine:

sin⁡P=oppositehypotenuse=QRPR=QR15

To find the length QR, we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

QR=PR2−PQ2=152−92=225−81=144=12

So we have

sin⁡P=QR15=1215=45,

and therefore csc⁡P=(45)−1=54.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Remember that $csc$ is the reciprocal of $sin.$ So first we need to compute sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡P=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac{QR}{PR}=\frac{QR}{15}
$$

To find the length $QR,$ we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

$$
\begin{aligned}QR & =\sqrt{P{R}^{2}-P{Q}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{15}^{2}-{9}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{225-81} \\  & =\sqrt{144} \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

So we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡P=\frac{QR}{15}=\frac{12}{15}=\frac{4}{5},
$$

and therefore

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡P={(\frac{4}{5})}^{-1}=\frac{5}{4}.
$$

Question 4
?

csc⁡P=

a
 157
b
 95
c
 85
d
 125
e
 54
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Remember that csc is the reciprocal of sin. So first we need to compute sine:

sin⁡P=oppositehypotenuse=QRPR=QR15

To find the length QR, we can use the Pythagorean Theorem:

QR=PR2−PQ2=152−92=225−81=144=12

So we have

sin⁡P=QR15=1215=45,

and therefore csc⁡P=(45)−1=54.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Solve the equation $\frac{2}{3x+2}=-\frac{4}{x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{2}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{3x+2}{2}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{6x+4}{4}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{6x+4}{4} & =4\cdot (-\frac{x}{4}) \\ 6x+4 & =-x \\ 6x+x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Solve the equation $\frac{1}{x+5}=\frac{1}{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=-5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+5}{1}=\frac{3}{1}
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
x+5=3
$$

We can now solve this equation using the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =3 \\ x+5-5 & =3-5 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Solve the equation $-\frac{4}{x-2}=\frac{1}{x-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{x-1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $4.$ The equation becomes

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{4x-4}{4}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot (\frac{x-2}{-4}) & =(-4)\cdot \frac{4x-4}{4} \\ x-2 & =-4x+4 \\ x+4x & =4+2 \\ 5x & =6 \\ (\frac{1}{5})\cdot (5x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})\cdot (\cancel{5}x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (6) \\ x & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
3.Solving Rational Equations with Binomials in Both Denominators?

Solve the equation −4x−2=1x−1.

M
Wed, Oct 14th @ 10:38 PM|Elapsed: 0:15Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{2}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{3x+2}{2}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{6x+4}{4}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{6x+4}{4} & =4\cdot (-\frac{x}{4}) \\ 6x+4 & =-x \\ 6x+x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

Question 3
?

Solve the equation −4x−2=1x−1.

a
53
b
−25
c
−5
d
56
e
65
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=2 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=1 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

−x−24=x−11

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, 4. The equation becomes −x−24=4x−44.

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: (−4)⋅(x−2−4)=(−4)⋅4x−44x−2=−4x+4x+4x=4+25x=6(15)⋅(5x)=(15)⋅(6)(15)⋅(5x)=(15)⋅(6)x=65

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Solve the equation $\frac{2}{3x+2}=-\frac{4}{x}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{2}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{3x+2}{2}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{6x+4}{4}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{6x+4}{4} & =4\cdot (-\frac{x}{4}) \\ 6x+4 & =-x \\ 6x+x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Solve the equation 23x+2=−4x.

a
37
b
74
c
32
d
−47
e
−12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=−23 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=0 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

3x+22=−x4

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator 4, as follows:

6x+44=−x4

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: 4⋅6x+44=4⋅(−x4)6x+4=−x6x+x=−4x=−47

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Solve the equation $\frac{2}{3x+2}=-\frac{4}{x}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=-\frac{2}{3}$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=0$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{3x+2}{2}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator $4,$ as follows:

$$
\frac{6x+4}{4}=-\frac{x}{4}
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot \frac{6x+4}{4} & =4\cdot (-\frac{x}{4}) \\ 6x+4 & =-x \\ 6x+x & =-4 \\ x & =-\frac{4}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Solve the equation $\frac{1}{x+5}=\frac{1}{3}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=-5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+5}{1}=\frac{3}{1}
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
x+5=3
$$

We can now solve this equation using the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =3 \\ x+5-5 & =3-5 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Solve the equation 1x+5=13.

a
−3
b
2
c
−2
d
5
e
3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that x=−5 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

x+51=31

The above equation simplifies to

x+5=3

We can now solve this equation using the addition principle:

x+5=3x+5−5=3−5x=−2

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: Solve the equation $\frac{1}{x+5}=\frac{1}{3}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that $x=-5$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero.

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
\frac{x+5}{1}=\frac{3}{1}
$$

The above equation simplifies to

$$
x+5=3
$$

We can now solve this equation using the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =3 \\ x+5-5 & =3-5 \\ x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Solve the equation $-\frac{4}{x-2}=\frac{1}{x-1}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{x-1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $4.$ The equation becomes

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{4x-4}{4}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot (\frac{x-2}{-4}) & =(-4)\cdot \frac{4x-4}{4} \\ x-2 & =-4x+4 \\ x+4x & =4+2 \\ 5x & =6 \\ (\frac{1}{5})\cdot (5x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})\cdot (\cancel{5}x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (6) \\ x & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3

Solve the equation −4x−2=1x−1.

a
53
b
−25
c
−5
d
56
e
65
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=2 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=1 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

−x−24=x−11

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, 4. The equation becomes −x−24=4x−44.

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: (−4)⋅(x−2−4)=(−4)⋅4x−44x−2=−4x+4x+4x=4+25x=6(15)⋅(5x)=(15)⋅(6)(15)⋅(5x)=(15)⋅(6)x=65

question.html:
Question 3
?

Solve the equation −4x−2=1x−1.

a
53
b
−25
c
−5
d
56
e
65
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

  • x=2 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

  • x=1 cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

ab=cd⟹ba=dc

The above technique works whenever a and c are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

−x−24=x−11

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, 4. The equation becomes −x−24=4x−44.

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles: (−4)⋅(x−2−4)=(−4)⋅4x−44x−2=−4x+4x+4x=4+25x=6(15)⋅(5x)=(15)⋅(6)(15)⋅(5x)=(15)⋅(6)x=65

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem: Solve the equation $-\frac{4}{x-2}=\frac{1}{x-1}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that

- $x=2$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the left-hand side zero

- $x=1$ cannot be a solution since this would make the denominator on the right-hand side zero

We can flip an equation involving two fractions as follows:

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{c}{d}\,⟹\,\frac{b}{a}=\frac{d}{c}
$$

The above technique works whenever $a$ and $c$ are both different from zero.

Therefore, we can flip the given equation as follows:

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{x-1}{1}
$$

Next, we write both fractions using the least common denominator, $4.$ The equation becomes

$$
-\frac{x-2}{4}=\frac{4x-4}{4}.
$$

We can now solve this equation with the addition and the multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4)\cdot (\frac{x-2}{-4}) & =(-4)\cdot \frac{4x-4}{4} \\ x-2 & =-4x+4 \\ x+4x & =4+2 \\ 5x & =6 \\ (\frac{1}{5})\cdot (5x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (6) \\ (\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})\cdot (\cancel{5}x) & =(\frac{1}{5})\cdot (6) \\ x & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨y(x-1),\,x(y-1)⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/b95320928a5e7482f9ba2b8bb1d1499950710545b4c7273b7f70dfe5ab8c84b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y(x-1)$ and $Q(x,y)=x(y-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((y-1)-(x-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/459a51f3c408a9c647b3be6b978267a6ce724e747118fbe897275c370d2bb6d6.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}r-2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/008f5dbaeb8c3c26008c49e97ed0490c444b049a991c2198399359a30b806b07.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2},\,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/c40d9fdfd10b3be4153c9c8ea3a6302af3cf0392533767313c467bdf7dcec1d7.png)

Since $P(x,y)={e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-2xy)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2-2xy)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{4}(2r-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
