questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/c1f8bb7ed82d345f8397ea9b01854f05f3f668acdcebf5d75ebbc5cb8de04fa6.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1})\,dy\,?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/9eceb8ab173995a8325fb1a8452baaa7f1071e569391e9a49b69c047d76f3b52.png)

Since $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/fb6a49b2172b3a60676ef74a244298eff05ffc65be6feca089c4a953757f2e59.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/66ab1a3e2e7244a9b3e5fc9bda814736194c28dd9438fbb97086e99be4633261.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-4{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{y}+4x{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/709d108b2b992d1714c7c0b3bef26f52e965c2467f38d05103cd45f4f9bc821b.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)=\sqrt{x}-4{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={e}^{y}+4x{y}^{2},
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-4{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{y}+4x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4{y}^{2}-(-4{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{r}^{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}16\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16[\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =16\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Given that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/1e78bf74df5607a1d80b3bd51b3222505e3bb201817448a7a5ebe5b0a73cffa9.svg)
where $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle y^2+\sin x, \: 3xy-\cos y  \right\rangle$ and $C$ is the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}
=
\oint\limits_{C} (y^2+\sin x) \: \mathrm{d}x + (3xy-\cos y) \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/798665574b8f0e11d991bb0d934efd01bdeb65840c2e86498be4edbc59578439.png)

Since $P(x,y)= y^2+\sin x$ and $Q(x,y)= 3xy-\cos y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,dx+(xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0\leq r \leq 2,\: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi  \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$

$$

$$

tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to evaluate the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\left( e^{-x^2}- x^2y \right) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left(y+xy^2\right) \mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $C$ is the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1,$ oriented counterclockwise. 

Direct evaluation of this integral is likely to be a difficult task. However, we can make light work of this tricky integral using Green's theorem.

Recall that Green's theorem states the following:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ (shown below) satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/dd859c753a8a5445eafab5db4f1e796b48997e1abb1728accd03fe3825e595d6.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y) = e^{-x^2}- x^2y, \qquad Q(x,y) = y+xy^2,
$$

we obtain the partial derivatives   

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{-{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(y+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

This double integral will be easier to evaluate if we switch to plane polar coordinates. 

The region $D$ in $xy$-coordinates can be represented as the region $\Delta$ in polar coordinates, given by

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral by applying the change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/b95320928a5e7482f9ba2b8bb1d1499950710545b4c7273b7f70dfe5ab8c84b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y(x-1)$ and $Q(x,y)=x(y-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((y-1)-(x-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ∮CF⋅dr=∫02π∫04AAAAAAAAdrdθ, where F(x,y)=⟨y(x−1),x(y−1)⟩ and C is the circle x2+y2=16 oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?

a
r2
b
r2(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)
c
r(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)
d
r2cos⁡(2θ)
e
rcos⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as

∮CF⋅dr=∮Cy(x−1)dx+x(y−1)dy.

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=y(x−1) and Q(x,y)=x(y−1), we obtain

∂P∂y=x−1,∂Q∂x=y−1.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮Cy(x−1)dx+x(y−1)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D((y−1)−(x−1))dA=∬D(y−x)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(y−x)dA=∬Δ(rsin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫02π∫04r2(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)drdθ.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/459a51f3c408a9c647b3be6b978267a6ce724e747118fbe897275c370d2bb6d6.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}r-2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given that ∮Cy2dx+xdy=∫02π∫01AAAAAAAAdrdθ, where C is the circle x2+y2=1 oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?

a
r−r2cos⁡θ
b
r−2r2sin⁡θ
c
r−r2sin⁡θ
d
r2sin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ
e
1−2rsin⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=y2 and Q(x,y)=x, we obtain

∂P∂y=2y,∂Q∂x=1.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮Cy2dx+xdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(1−2y)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤1,0≤θ≤2π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(1−2y)dA=∬Δ(1−2⋅rsin⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫02π∫01r−2r2sin⁡θdrdθ.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem

observed_steps.name: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}
=
\oint\limits_{C} (2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left( e^{y/3} + 3x \right) \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/e4c7913793a4b08916a832e575c5b2c167d5dfeec244eea23857731df1e514e7.png)

Since $P(x,y)= 2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}$ and $Q(x,y)=e^{y/3} + 3x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2y+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x+5}))\,dx+({e}^{y/3}+3x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \right\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/ffaf242238a8d32ce0f134cff6e0cf4256b2888b0a71f65e3c5ec470cbce284a.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above and the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle 2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}, \: e^{y/3} + 3x \right\rangle.$ 
Find a repeated integral in plane polar coordinates that's equivalent to $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \, .$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}
=
\oint\limits_{C} (2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left( e^{y/3} + 3x \right) \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/e4c7913793a4b08916a832e575c5b2c167d5dfeec244eea23857731df1e514e7.png)

Since $P(x,y)= 2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}$ and $Q(x,y)=e^{y/3} + 3x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2y+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x+5}))\,dx+({e}^{y/3}+3x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \right\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/c40d9fdfd10b3be4153c9c8ea3a6302af3cf0392533767313c467bdf7dcec1d7.png)

Since $P(x,y)={e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-2xy)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2-2xy)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{4}(2r-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Consider the path C shown above. Given that F(x,y)=⟨ex/4+xy2,esin⁡y+2x⟩, which of the following is equivalent to ∮CF⋅dr?

a
∫03π/2∫04(resin⁡θ−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
b
∫−π/20∫04(2resin⁡θ−r2sin⁡θ)drdθ
c
∫−π/20∫04(2r−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
d
∫03π/2∫04(2r−r2sin⁡θ)drdθ
e
∫−π/20∫04(2r−r2sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as

∮CF⋅dr=∮C(ex/4+xy2)dx+(esin⁡y+2x)dy.

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=ex/4+xy2 and Q(x,y)=esin⁡y+2x, we obtain

∂P∂y=2xy,∂Q∂x=2.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮C(ex/4+xy2)dx+(esin⁡y+2x)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(2−2xy)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤4,−π2≤θ≤0}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(2−2xy)dA=∬Δ(2−2⋅rcos⁡θ⋅rsin⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫−π/20∫04(2r−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/9eceb8ab173995a8325fb1a8452baaa7f1071e569391e9a49b69c047d76f3b52.png)

Since $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Consider the path C shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral ∮C(sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y)dx+(xy2−1y+1)dy?

a
∫0π∫02(r+sin⁡(cos⁡θ))drdθ
b
∫−π/2π/2∫03r3drdθ
c
∫0π∫03rdrdθ
d
∫−π/2π/2∫03rdrdθ
e
∫0π∫03r3drdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y and Q(x,y)=xy2−1y+1, we obtain

∂P∂y=−x2,∂Q∂x=y2.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮C(sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y)dx+(xy2−1y+1)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(y2−(−x2))dA=∬D(x2+y2)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤3,0≤θ≤π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(x2+y2)dA=∬Δ(r2cos2⁡θ+r2sin2⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫0π∫03r3drdθ.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/709d108b2b992d1714c7c0b3bef26f52e965c2467f38d05103cd45f4f9bc821b.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)=\sqrt{x}-4{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={e}^{y}+4x{y}^{2},
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-4{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{y}+4x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4{y}^{2}-(-4{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{r}^{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}16\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16[\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =16\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

judgments.reasoning: The earlier answer b was graded Correct and matches the worked solution. Green's theorem gives Q_x-P_y=y-x; polar substitution and the Jacobian r give r^2(\sin\theta-\cos\theta).

The earlier selection b was graded Correct and agrees with the worked solution. Green's theorem gives 1-2y; polar substitution and the Jacobian give (1-2r\sin\theta)r=r-2r^2\sin\theta. Options a and c incidentally have the same total integral, but b is the direct transformed integrand.

The earlier selection c was graded Correct and matches the worked solution. Green's theorem gives Q_x-P_y=2-2xy. On the positively oriented fourth-quadrant quarter disk, polar substitution gives (2-2xy)r=2r-r^3\sin(2\theta), with 0≤r≤4 and -\pi/2≤\theta≤0.

The earlier selection e was graded Correct and matches the worked solution. Green's theorem gives Q_x-P_y=x^2+y^2, so the upper half disk yields the integrand r^3 with 0≤r≤3 and 0≤\theta≤\pi. The answer is valid, although not unique under literal numerical equivalence: option b also evaluates to 81\pi/4.

Math Academy graded option a, 8, Correct, confirming the intended answer. My earlier domain objection remains: C contains an interval with y<-3^{1/7}, where y^7+3<0, so the real line integral is undefined. Formally integrating Q_x-P_y=4xy over the pictured region gives 8, but Green's theorem cannot justify this for the stated real field. The worked solution also mistakenly replaces x^2 with \sqrt{x} in one line.

The earlier selection c, 8\pi, was graded Correct and matches the worked solution. The exact differential terms \sqrt{x}\,dx and e^y\,dy contribute zero. Green's theorem applied to the remaining polynomial terms gives \int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^2 4r^3\,dr\,d\theta=8\pi.

The missing expression is r^2\sin\theta, agreeing with Math Academy's stated answer. Green's theorem gives Q_x-P_y=3y-2y=y, and polar substitution contributes another factor r. The worked solution contains a transcription error: its 'Applying Green's theorem' display uses xy-\cos y instead of 3xy-\cos y. The subsequent calculation and final answer use the original field correctly. No answer fields are supplied for this example.

Math Academy's repeated integral, \int_{\pi/2}^{2\pi}\int_0^3 r\,dr\,d\theta, is correct. The arrows positively orient the three-quarter disk excluding the first quadrant. Green's theorem gives Q_x-P_y=3-2=1, and the polar Jacobian supplies r. The field is smooth on a neighborhood of the region because x+5≥2 there. The integral evaluates to 27\pi/4. No answer fields are supplied for this example.

The screenshot states 12\pi, which is correct. With P=e^{-x^2}-y^3 and Q=e^{-y^2}+x^3, Green's theorem gives Q_x-P_y=3(x^2+y^2). The positively oriented upper half disk has 0≤r≤2 and 0≤\theta≤\pi, so the integral is \int_0^\pi\int_0^2 3r^3\,dr\,d\theta=12\pi. No answer fields are supplied for this example.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨y(x-1),\,x(y-1)⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/b95320928a5e7482f9ba2b8bb1d1499950710545b4c7273b7f70dfe5ab8c84b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y(x-1)$ and $Q(x,y)=x(y-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((y-1)-(x-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that ∮CF⋅dr=∫02π∫04AAAAAAAAdrdθ, where F(x,y)=⟨y(x−1),x(y−1)⟩ and C is the circle x2+y2=16 oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?

a
r2
b
r2(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)
c
r(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)
d
r2cos⁡(2θ)
e
rcos⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as

∮CF⋅dr=∮Cy(x−1)dx+x(y−1)dy.

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=y(x−1) and Q(x,y)=x(y−1), we obtain

∂P∂y=x−1,∂Q∂x=y−1.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮Cy(x−1)dx+x(y−1)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D((y−1)−(x−1))dA=∬D(y−x)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤4,0≤θ≤2π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(y−x)dA=∬Δ(rsin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫02π∫04r2(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)drdθ.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/b95320928a5e7482f9ba2b8bb1d1499950710545b4c7273b7f70dfe5ab8c84b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y(x-1)$ and $Q(x,y)=x(y-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((y-1)-(x-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that ∮CF⋅dr=∫02π∫04AAAAAAAAdrdθ, where F(x,y)=⟨y(x−1),x(y−1)⟩ and C is the circle x2+y2=16 oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?

a
r2
b
r2(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)
c
r(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)
d
r2cos⁡(2θ)
e
rcos⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as

∮CF⋅dr=∮Cy(x−1)dx+x(y−1)dy.

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=y(x−1) and Q(x,y)=x(y−1), we obtain

∂P∂y=x−1,∂Q∂x=y−1.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮Cy(x−1)dx+x(y−1)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D((y−1)−(x−1))dA=∬D(y−x)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤4,0≤θ≤2π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(y−x)dA=∬Δ(rsin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫02π∫04r2(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)drdθ.

solution.reasoning: Green's theorem gives Q_x-P_y=(y-1)-(x-1)=y-x. Substituting x=r\cos\theta, y=r\sin\theta and including the polar Jacobian r gives r^2(\sin\theta-\cos\theta), option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes the current question's key.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem:
Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨y(x-1),\,x(y-1)⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/b95320928a5e7482f9ba2b8bb1d1499950710545b4c7273b7f70dfe5ab8c84b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y(x-1)$ and $Q(x,y)=x(y-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((y-1)-(x-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
question.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/459a51f3c408a9c647b3be6b978267a6ce724e747118fbe897275c370d2bb6d6.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}r-2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given that ∮Cy2dx+xdy=∫02π∫01AAAAAAAAdrdθ, where C is the circle x2+y2=1 oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?

a
r−r2cos⁡θ
b
r−2r2sin⁡θ
c
r−r2sin⁡θ
d
r2sin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ
e
1−2rsin⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=y2 and Q(x,y)=x, we obtain

∂P∂y=2y,∂Q∂x=1.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮Cy2dx+xdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(1−2y)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤1,0≤θ≤2π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(1−2y)dA=∬Δ(1−2⋅rsin⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫02π∫01r−2r2sin⁡θdrdθ.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/459a51f3c408a9c647b3be6b978267a6ce724e747118fbe897275c370d2bb6d6.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}r-2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given that ∮Cy2dx+xdy=∫02π∫01AAAAAAAAdrdθ, where C is the circle x2+y2=1 oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?

a
r−r2cos⁡θ
b
r−2r2sin⁡θ
c
r−r2sin⁡θ
d
r2sin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ
e
1−2rsin⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=y2 and Q(x,y)=x, we obtain

∂P∂y=2y,∂Q∂x=1.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮Cy2dx+xdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(1−2y)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤1,0≤θ≤2π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(1−2y)dA=∬Δ(1−2⋅rsin⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫02π∫01r−2r2sin⁡θdrdθ.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem

solution.reasoning: With P=y^2 and Q=x, Green's theorem gives Q_x-P_y=1-2y. Substituting y=r\sin\theta and multiplying by the polar Jacobian r gives r-2r^2\sin\theta, option b. This is the intended transformed integrand; options a and c incidentally give the same total integral by symmetry. No answer key or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
feedback.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/459a51f3c408a9c647b3be6b978267a6ce724e747118fbe897275c370d2bb6d6.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}r-2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/008f5dbaeb8c3c26008c49e97ed0490c444b049a991c2198399359a30b806b07.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2},\,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/c40d9fdfd10b3be4153c9c8ea3a6302af3cf0392533767313c467bdf7dcec1d7.png)

Since $P(x,y)={e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-2xy)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$

$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Consider the path C shown above. Given that F(x,y)=⟨ex/4+xy2,esin⁡y+2x⟩, which of the following is equivalent to ∮CF⋅dr?

a
∫03π/2∫04(resin⁡θ−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
b
∫−π/20∫04(2resin⁡θ−r2sin⁡θ)drdθ
c
∫−π/20∫04(2r−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
d
∫03π/2∫04(2r−r2sin⁡θ)drdθ
e
∫−π/20∫04(2r−r2sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as

∮CF⋅dr=∮C(ex/4+xy2)dx+(esin⁡y+2x)dy.

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=ex/4+xy2 and Q(x,y)=esin⁡y+2x, we obtain

∂P∂y=2xy,∂Q∂x=2.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮C(ex/4+xy2)dx+(esin⁡y+2x)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(2−2xy)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤4,−π2≤θ≤0}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(2−2xy)dA=∬Δ(2−2⋅rcos⁡θ⋅rsin⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫−π/20∫04(2r−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/c40d9fdfd10b3be4153c9c8ea3a6302af3cf0392533767313c467bdf7dcec1d7.png)

Since $P(x,y)={e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-2xy)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2-2xy)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{4}(2r-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Consider the path C shown above. Given that F(x,y)=⟨ex/4+xy2,esin⁡y+2x⟩, which of the following is equivalent to ∮CF⋅dr?

a
∫03π/2∫04(resin⁡θ−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
b
∫−π/20∫04(2resin⁡θ−r2sin⁡θ)drdθ
c
∫−π/20∫04(2r−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
d
∫03π/2∫04(2r−r2sin⁡θ)drdθ
e
∫−π/20∫04(2r−r2sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as

∮CF⋅dr=∮C(ex/4+xy2)dx+(esin⁡y+2x)dy.

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=ex/4+xy2 and Q(x,y)=esin⁡y+2x, we obtain

∂P∂y=2xy,∂Q∂x=2.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮C(ex/4+xy2)dx+(esin⁡y+2x)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(2−2xy)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤4,−π2≤θ≤0}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(2−2xy)dA=∬Δ(2−2⋅rcos⁡θ⋅rsin⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫−π/20∫04(2r−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem

solution.reasoning: The arrows positively orient the fourth-quadrant quarter disk, so 0≤r≤4 and -\pi/2≤\theta≤0. Green's theorem gives Q_x-P_y=2-2xy. Using 2xy=r^2\sin(2\theta) and the Jacobian r yields 2r-r^3\sin(2\theta), which is option c. No captured answer or grade establishes Math Academy's key for this question.

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/008f5dbaeb8c3c26008c49e97ed0490c444b049a991c2198399359a30b806b07.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2},\,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/c40d9fdfd10b3be4153c9c8ea3a6302af3cf0392533767313c467bdf7dcec1d7.png)

Since $P(x,y)={e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x/4}+x{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}+2x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-2xy)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2-2xy)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{4}(2r-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 3
?

Consider the path C shown above. Given that F(x,y)=⟨ex/4+xy2,esin⁡y+2x⟩, which of the following is equivalent to ∮CF⋅dr?

a
∫03π/2∫04(resin⁡θ−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
b
∫−π/20∫04(2resin⁡θ−r2sin⁡θ)drdθ
c
∫−π/20∫04(2r−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
d
∫03π/2∫04(2r−r2sin⁡θ)drdθ
e
∫−π/20∫04(2r−r2sin⁡(2θ))drdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as

∮CF⋅dr=∮C(ex/4+xy2)dx+(esin⁡y+2x)dy.

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=ex/4+xy2 and Q(x,y)=esin⁡y+2x, we obtain

∂P∂y=2xy,∂Q∂x=2.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮C(ex/4+xy2)dx+(esin⁡y+2x)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(2−2xy)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤4,−π2≤θ≤0}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(2−2xy)dA=∬Δ(2−2⋅rcos⁡θ⋅rsin⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫−π/20∫04(2r−r3sin⁡(2θ))drdθ.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/c1f8bb7ed82d345f8397ea9b01854f05f3f668acdcebf5d75ebbc5cb8de04fa6.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1})\,dy\,?
$$
question.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/9eceb8ab173995a8325fb1a8452baaa7f1071e569391e9a49b69c047d76f3b52.png)

Since $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the path C shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral ∮C(sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y)dx+(xy2−1y+1)dy?

a
∫0π∫02(r+sin⁡(cos⁡θ))drdθ
b
∫−π/2π/2∫03r3drdθ
c
∫0π∫03rdrdθ
d
∫−π/2π/2∫03rdrdθ
e
∫0π∫03r3drdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y and Q(x,y)=xy2−1y+1, we obtain

∂P∂y=−x2,∂Q∂x=y2.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮C(sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y)dx+(xy2−1y+1)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(y2−(−x2))dA=∬D(x2+y2)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤3,0≤θ≤π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(x2+y2)dA=∬Δ(r2cos2⁡θ+r2sin2⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫0π∫03r3drdθ.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
last_observation.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/9eceb8ab173995a8325fb1a8452baaa7f1071e569391e9a49b69c047d76f3b52.png)

Since $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1})\,dy\,?

question.html:
Question 4
?

Consider the path C shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral ∮C(sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y)dx+(xy2−1y+1)dy?

a
∫0π∫02(r+sin⁡(cos⁡θ))drdθ
b
∫−π/2π/2∫03r3drdθ
c
∫0π∫03rdrdθ
d
∫−π/2π/2∫03rdrdθ
e
∫0π∫03r3drdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y and Q(x,y)=xy2−1y+1, we obtain

∂P∂y=−x2,∂Q∂x=y2.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮C(sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y)dx+(xy2−1y+1)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(y2−(−x2))dA=∬D(x2+y2)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤3,0≤θ≤π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(x2+y2)dA=∬Δ(r2cos2⁡θ+r2sin2⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫0π∫03r3drdθ.
question.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem

solution.reasoning: Green's theorem gives Q_x-P_y=y^2+x^2=r^2. The arrows positively orient the upper half disk, with 0≤r≤3 and 0≤\theta≤\pi. Including the Jacobian r gives option e, whose value is 81\pi/4. Option b also has this numerical value because the integrand is independent of \theta and its angular interval also has length \pi, so the literal equivalence question admits both. Option e represents the pictured region directly. No current Math Academy key or grade is captured.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/c1f8bb7ed82d345f8397ea9b01854f05f3f668acdcebf5d75ebbc5cb8de04fa6.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1})\,dy\,?
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/9eceb8ab173995a8325fb1a8452baaa7f1071e569391e9a49b69c047d76f3b52.png)

Since $P(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{y+1})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the path C shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral ∮C(sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y)dx+(xy2−1y+1)dy?

a
∫0π∫02(r+sin⁡(cos⁡θ))drdθ
b
∫−π/2π/2∫03r3drdθ
c
∫0π∫03rdrdθ
d
∫−π/2π/2∫03rdrdθ
e
∫0π∫03r3drdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y and Q(x,y)=xy2−1y+1, we obtain

∂P∂y=−x2,∂Q∂x=y2.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮C(sin⁡(cos⁡x)−x2y)dx+(xy2−1y+1)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(y2−(−x2))dA=∬D(x2+y2)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤3,0≤θ≤π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(x2+y2)dA=∬Δ(r2cos2⁡θ+r2sin2⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫0π∫03r3drdθ.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/fb6a49b2172b3a60676ef74a244298eff05ffc65be6feca089c4a953757f2e59.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}({x}^{2}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above.
question.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/d816d9153e22dd109e20e3e387f6a0028e3f6a9eaf1d284dfae8b5fdf54cfc6e.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2},\,Q(x,y)=\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y,
$$

 we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-x{y}^{2})dx+(\sqrt{{y}^{7}+3}+{x}^{2}y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy-(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =4[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0] \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/66ab1a3e2e7244a9b3e5fc9bda814736194c28dd9438fbb97086e99be4633261.png)

Evaluate ${∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-4{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{y}+4x{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where the path $C$ is shown above.
feedback.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224501/assets/709d108b2b992d1714c7c0b3bef26f52e965c2467f38d05103cd45f4f9bc821b.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)=\sqrt{x}-4{x}^{2}y,\,Q(x,y)={e}^{y}+4x{y}^{2},
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\sqrt{x}-4{x}^{2}y)dx+({e}^{y}+4x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4{y}^{2}-(-4{x}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}4({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}4({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{r}^{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}16\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =16[\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =16\cdot \frac{\pi }{2} \\  & =8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: What is the volume of a rectangular solid that has length, width, and height of $9\,\text{ft},$ $4\,\text{ft},$ and $5\,\text{ft},$ respectively?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=9\,\text{ft},\,w=4\,\text{ft},\,h=5\,\text{ft}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
V=9\cdot 4\cdot 5=180\,{\text{ft}}^{3}.
$$

questions.problem: What is the volume of a rectangular solid that has length, width, and height of $2\sqrt{2}\,\text{m},$ $4\,\text{m},$ and $3\sqrt{3}\,\text{m},$ respectively?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=2\sqrt{2}\,\text{m},\,w=4\,\text{m},\,h=3\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
V=2\sqrt{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3\sqrt{3}=24\sqrt{6}\,{\text{m}}^{3}.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224606/assets/175d15b140a660148d8890cf32f4c4b79a43ff86d82c7e4461174326dfa9eeca.png)

Find the volume of the rectangular prism shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=7\,\text{in},\,w=2\,\text{in},\,h=3\,\text{in}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
V=7\cdot 2\cdot 3=42\,{\text{in}}^{3}.
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: What is the volume of a rectangular solid that has length, width, and height of $\sqrt{5}\,\text{ft},$ $\sqrt{10}\,\text{ft},$ and $2\,\text{ft},$ respectively?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=\sqrt{5}\,\text{ft},\,w=\sqrt{10}\,\text{ft},\,h=2\,\text{ft}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
V=\sqrt{5}\cdot \sqrt{10}\cdot 2=2\sqrt{50}=10\sqrt{2}\,{\text{ft}}^{3}.
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: What is the volume of a rectangular solid that has length, width, and height of $7\,\text{cm},$ $\sqrt{5}\,\text{cm},$ and $2\sqrt{5}\,\text{cm},$ respectively?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=7\,\text{cm},\,w=\sqrt{5}\,\text{cm},\,h=2\sqrt{5}\,\text{cm}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
V=7\cdot \sqrt{5}\cdot 2\sqrt{5}=14\sqrt{25}=70\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: The height of a rectangular solid is $2\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}$ and its volume is $24\sqrt{3}\,{\text{m}}^{3}.$ If the base  (length × width) of the solid is a square, find the length of the solid.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Since the base of the rectangular solid is a square, we have that 

$$
l=w.
$$

Substituting 

$$
V=24\sqrt{3},\,h=2\sqrt{3},\,w=l
$$

into the formula, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =lwh \\ V & ={l}^{2}h \\ 24\sqrt{3} & ={l}^{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{3} \\ {l}^{2} & =12 \\ l & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length is $2\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}.$

Determine the length of the rectangular solid above given that its volume is $84\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
V=84,\,w=3\sqrt{2},\,h=\sqrt{8}
$$

into the formula, we obtain the following

$$
\begin{aligned}84 & =l\cdot 3\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{8} \\ 84 & =3\sqrt{16}l \\ 84 & =12l \\ l & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length is $7\,\text{cm}.$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: The height of a rectangular solid is $15\,\text{cm}$ and its volume is $675\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ If the base of the solid is a square, find the length of the solid.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Since the base of the rectangular solid is a square, we have that 

$$
l=w.
$$

Substituting 

$$
V=675,\,h=15,\,w=l
$$

into the formula, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =lwh \\ V & ={l}^{2}h \\ 675 & ={l}^{2}\cdot 15 \\ {l}^{2} & =45 \\ l & =3\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length is $3\sqrt{5}\,\text{cm}.$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224606/assets/70fc259b5863513eabaf6b67eeb5e6b8debcb40d4a91d096f6515cb9f2efe642.png)

Determine the length of the rectangular solid above given that its volume is $720\,{\text{in}}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
V=720,\,w=5,\,h=8
$$

into the formula, we obtain the following

$$
\begin{aligned}720 & =l\cdot 5\cdot 8 \\ 720 & =40l \\ l & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length is $18\,\text{in}.$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: A bar of chocolate in the form of a rectangular prism is $9\,\text{cm}$ long, $5\,\text{cm}$ wide, and $2\,\text{cm}$ high. If the chocolate costs $$0.02$ per cubic centimeter, what is the value of four identical bars of chocolate?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the volume of the bar of chocolate.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=9,\,w=5,\,h=2
$$

into the formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}V=9\cdot 5\cdot 2=90\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The total volume of the four bars of chocolate is

$$
90\cdot 4=360\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

Finally, the cost of four chocolate bars is

$$
360\cdot 0.02=$7.20.
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem: A person has seven identical boxes in the form of a rectangular solid. Each box is $10\,\text{in}$ long, $8\,\text{in}$ wide, and $8\,\text{in}$ high. What is the total combined volume of the boxes?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the volume of one box.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=10,\,w=8,\,h=8
$$

into the formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}V=10\cdot 8\cdot 8=640\,{\text{in}}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total volume of the seven storage boxes is

$$
640\cdot 7=4\,480\,{\text{in}}^{3}.
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem: A shipping company delivered six identical packages in the form of a rectangular prism. Each package is $40\,\text{cm}$ long, $20\,\text{cm}$ wide, and $10\,\text{cm}$ high. What is the total combined volume of the packages?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the volume of one package.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=40,\,w=20,\,h=10
$$

into the formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}V=40\cdot 20\cdot 10=8\,000\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total volume of the six packages is

$$
8\,000\cdot 6=48\,000\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14224606/assets/6240abf268497f82475003619689d979b0b00678b4d49972ff2fbcf1fa866a9c.png)

The diagram above shows a cubic gas tank. One-fifth of the volume of the tank is filled with gas. If the fuel costs $$0.0016$ per cubic centimeter, how much would it cost to fill the tank to capacity?
questions.worked_solution:
The length of $7\,\text{cm}$ shown in the diagram represents one-fifth of the tank's side length. Therefore, the length of each side of the tank is

$$
5\cdot 7=35\,\text{cm}.
$$

The empty space in the cube is a rectangular prism that is $35\,\text{cm}$ long, $35\,\text{cm}$ wide, and $35-7=28\,\text{cm}$ high.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=35\,\text{cm},\,w=35\,\text{cm},\,h=28\,\text{cm}
$$

into the formula, we obtain

$$
V=35\cdot 35\cdot 28=34\,300\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

Finally, to fill the tank to capacity, it would cost

$$
34\,300\cdot 0.0016=$54.88.
$$
