last_observation.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)={y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot y \\  & ={A}^{T}(Ax-b) \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -7 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -29\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function L:R2→R defined by L(x)=12(Ax−b)T(Ax−b) where A=[312450],b=[678]. What is ∇xL(x) at x=[2−1]?

b

EXPLANATION

We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let y=Ax−b. Then, L(x)=12yTy, and

∇xL=(dLdx)T=(dydx)T⋅(dLdy)T.

Now, since

ddy(12yTy)=yTanddydx=ddx(Ax−b)=A,

we have that

∇xL=(dydx)T⋅(dLdy)T=AT⋅y.

Evaluating at x=[2−1], we get

∇xL=AT⋅y=AT(Ax−b)=[312450]T([312450]⋅[2−1]−[678])=[325140]([5010]−[678])=[325140][−1−72]=[−7−29].

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}(Ax-b)^{T}(Ax-b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-b.$ Then, $L(x)=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{1}{2}{y}^{T}y)={y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot y \\  & ={A}^{T}(Ax-b) \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ 10\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -7 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -29\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=(Ax-2b)^{T}(Ax-2b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-2b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-2b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & =2\cdot {A}^{T}(Ax-2b) \\  & =2\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}58 \\ 26\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the function L:R2→R defined by L(x)=(Ax−2b)T(Ax−2b) where A=[32−1112],b=[135]. What is ∇xL(x) at x=[14]?

a
[2115]
b
[5826]
c
[5826]
d
[3042]
e
[3042]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let y=Ax−2b. Then, L(x)=yTy, and

∇xL=(dLdx)T=(dydx)T⋅(dLdy)T.

Now, since

ddy(yTy)=2yTanddydx=ddx(Ax−2b)=A,

we have that

∇xL=(dydx)T⋅(dLdy)T=AT⋅2y.

Evaluating at x=[14], we get

∇xL=AT⋅2y=2⋅AT(Ax−2b)=2⋅[32−1112]T([32−1112]⋅[14]−2⋅[135])=2⋅[3−11212]([1139]−[2610])=[6−22424][9−3−1]=[5826].

$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-2b)=A,

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & =2\cdot {A}^{T}(Ax-2b) \\  & =2\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}58 \\ 26\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the function L:R2→R defined by L(x)=(Ax−2b)T(Ax−2b) where A=[32−1112],b=[135]. What is ∇xL(x) at x=[14]?

a
[2115]
b
[5826]

[5826]
d
[3042]
e
[3042]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let y=Ax−2b. Then, L(x)=yTy, and

∇xL=(dLdx)T=(dydx)T⋅(dLdy)T.

Now, since

ddy(yTy)=2yTanddydx=ddx(Ax−2b)=A,

we have that

∇xL=(dydx)T⋅(dLdy)T=AT⋅2y.

Evaluating at x=[14], we get

∇xL=AT⋅2y=2⋅AT(Ax−2b)=2⋅[32−1112]T([32−1112]⋅[14]−2⋅[135])=2⋅[3−11212]([1139]−[2610])=[6−22424][9−3−1]=[5826].

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Consider the function $L:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $L(x)=(Ax-2b)^{T}(Ax-2b)$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

What is ${∇}_{x}L(x)$ at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We can solve this problem by applying the chain rule for gradients.

Let $y=Ax-2b.$ Then, $L(x)={y}^{T}y,$ and

$$
{∇}_{x}L={(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}x})}^{T}={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{T}y)=2{y}^{T}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(Ax-2b)=A,
$$

we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot {(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}y})}^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}L & ={A}^{T}\cdot 2y \\  & =2\cdot {A}^{T}(Ax-2b) \\  & =2\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}([\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]) \\  & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]([\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ 10\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}58 \\ 26\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]x $$ with respect to $x$ at $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}.$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+2 \\ 0-4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]x $$ with respect to $x$ at $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}.$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+2 \\ 0-4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

f(x)=xT[10−22]x
with respect to x at x=[0−1]T.

∇xf=
0
−4

Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Defining the matrix A as
A=[10−22], we have f(x)=xTAx.

Since A is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function: ∇xf(x)=(AT+A)x

First, we compute AT=[1−202], which gives AT+A=[1−202]+[10−22]=[2−2−24].

Now, compute the gradient at x=[0−1]:

∇xf(x)=(AT+A)x=[2−2−24][0−1]=[0+20−4]=[2−4]

solution.reasoning: For f(x)=x^TAx, ∇f(x)=(A+A^T)x. Here A+A^T has rows (2,-2) and (-2,4), so at x=(0,-1)^T the gradient is (2,-4)^T. No captured Math Academy answer evidence establishes its key.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Compute the gradient of the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by $$ f(x)={x}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}]x $$ with respect to $x$ at $x={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}.$
$\,{∇}_{x}f=\,\,$ {{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
Defining the matrix $A$ as

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}],
$$

we have $f(x)={x}^{T}Ax.$

Since $A$ is not symmetric, we use the more general formula for the gradient of a quadratic function:

$$
{∇}_{x}f(x)=({A}^{T}+A)x
$$

First, we compute

$$
{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}],
$$

which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}+A & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -4 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 1 & -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, compute the gradient at $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x}f(x) & =({A}^{T}+A)x \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 1 \\ 1 & -10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0+1 \\ 0-10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Suppose that 

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}n}{n!}
$$

and that ${s}_{5}$ is the fifth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-{s}_{5}|<k$ for some real number $k.$ Find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=\frac{n}{n!}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}n}{n!}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is positive and decreasing for $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $5$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{5}|<|{b}_{6}|=|\frac{(-1)^{6}\cdot 6}{6!}|=\frac{6}{720}=\frac{1}{120}.
$$

 

Therefore, $k=\frac{1}{120}.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Given that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}-1}
$$

and that ${s}_{i}$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of $i$ such that $|S-{s}_{i}|<0.1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{n}^{2}-1}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}-1}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing for $n\ge 2$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test. 

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{i}|<|{b}_{i+1}|.
$$

So, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}|{b}_{i+1}|=|\frac{(-1)^{i+1}}{(i+1)^{2}-1}| & \le 0.1 \\ \frac{1}{{i}^{2}+2i+1-1} & \le \frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{1}{{i}^{2}+2i} & \le \frac{1}{10} \\ {i}^{2}+2i & \ge 10.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Given that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{2}^{n}}
$$

and that ${s}_{i}$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of $i$ such that $|S-{s}_{i}|<0.01.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{2}^{n}}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{2}^{n}}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing for $n\ge 1$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test. 

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{i}|<|{b}_{i+1}|.
$$

So, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}|{b}_{i+1}|=|\frac{(-1)^{i+1}}{{2}^{i+1}}| & \le 0.01 \\ \frac{1}{{2}^{i+1}} & \le \frac{1}{100} \\ 100 & \le {2}^{i+1} \\ 100 & \le 2\cdot {2}^{i} \\ {2}^{i} & \ge 50.\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{e}^{n+2}}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{e}^{n+2}}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is positive and decreasing for $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

$$
|S-{s}_{6}|<|{b}_{7}|=|\frac{{(-1)}^{7}}{{e}^{7+2}}|=\frac{1}{{e}^{9}}.
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{1}{{e}^{9}}.$

Question 1
?

Suppose that S=∑n=1∞(−1)nnn! and that s5 is the fifth partial sum of S. According to the alternating series error bound, |S−s5|<k for some real number k. Find the value of k.

a
16
b
1720
c
1120
d
160
e
15
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let an=nn! and bn=(−1)nnn!. Then an is positive and decreasing for n≥1, and an→0 as n→∞. So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the 5th partial sum, it states that

|S−s5|<|b6|=|(−1)6⋅66!|=6720=1120.

Therefore, k=1120.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{n}^{2}-1}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}-1}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing for $n\ge 2$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test. 

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{i}|<|{b}_{i+1}|.
$$

So, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}|{b}_{i+1}|=|\frac{(-1)^{i+1}}{(i+1)^{2}-1}| & \le 0.1 \\ \frac{1}{{i}^{2}+2i+1-1} & \le \frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{1}{{i}^{2}+2i} & \le \frac{1}{10} \\ {i}^{2}+2i & \ge 10.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Suppose that 

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}n}{n!}
$$

and that ${s}_{5}$ is the fifth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-{s}_{5}|<k$ for some real number $k.$ Find the value of $k.$
question.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=\frac{n}{n!}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}n}{n!}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is positive and decreasing for $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $5$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{5}|<|{b}_{6}|=|\frac{(-1)^{6}\cdot 6}{6!}|=\frac{6}{720}=\frac{1}{120}.

question.html:
Question 1
?

Suppose that S=∑n=1∞(−1)nnn! and that s5 is the fifth partial sum of S. According to the alternating series error bound, |S−s5|<k for some real number k. Find the value of k.

a
16
b
1720
c
1120
d
160
e
15
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let an=nn! and bn=(−1)nnn!. Then an is positive and decreasing for n≥1, and an→0 as n→∞. So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the 5th partial sum, it states that

|S−s5|<|b6|=|(−1)6⋅66!|=6720=1120.

Therefore, k=1120.

solution.reasoning: The alternating series error bound uses the first omitted term: k = 6/6! = 1/120. Thus |S-s_5| < 1/120, giving option c. Mathematical confidence is high; no captured Math Academy answer evidence establishes its key.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem:
Suppose that 

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}n}{n!}
$$

and that ${s}_{5}$ is the fifth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-{s}_{5}|<k$ for some real number $k.$ Find the value of $k.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=\frac{n}{n!}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}n}{n!}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is positive and decreasing for $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $5$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{5}|<|{b}_{6}|=|\frac{(-1)^{6}\cdot 6}{6!}|=\frac{6}{720}=\frac{1}{120}.
$$

 

Therefore, $k=\frac{1}{120}.$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Given that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}-1}
$$

and that ${s}_{i}$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of $i$ such that $|S-{s}_{i}|<0.1.$
question.worked_solution:
First, let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{n}^{2}-1}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}-1}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing for $n\ge 2$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test. 

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{i}|<|{b}_{i+1}|.
$$

So, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}|{b}_{i+1}|=|\frac{(-1)^{i+1}}{(i+1)^{2}-1}| & \le 0.1 \\ \frac{1}{{i}^{2}+2i+1-1} & \le \frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{1}{{i}^{2}+2i} & \le \frac{1}{10} \\ {i}^{2}+2i & \ge 10.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{n}^{2}-1}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}-1}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing for $n\ge 2$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test. 

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{i}|<|{b}_{i+1}|.
$$

So, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}|{b}_{i+1}|=|\frac{(-1)^{i+1}}{(i+1)^{2}-1}| & \le 0.1 \\ \frac{1}{{i}^{2}+2i+1-1} & \le \frac{1}{10} \\ \frac{1}{{i}^{2}+2i} & \le \frac{1}{10} \\ {i}^{2}+2i & \ge 10.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Given that S=∑n=2∞(−1)nn2−1 and that si is the ith partial sum of S, use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of i such that |S−si|<0.1.

a
i2+4i≥98
b
i2+2i≥8
c
i2+4i≥10
d
i2+2i≥10
e
i2+2i≥100
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let an=1n2−1 and bn=(−1)nn2−1. Then an is decreasing for n≥2 and an→0 as n→∞. So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the ith partial sum, it states that |S−si|<|bi+1|.

So, we require

|bi+1|=|(−1)i+1(i+1)2−1|≤0.11i2+2i+1−1≤1101i2+2i≤110i2+2i≥10.

solution.reasoning: Using the truncation convention s_i = sum from n=2 through n=i, the first omitted magnitude is 1/((i+1)^2-1) = 1/(i^2+2i). The alternating series bound guarantees the requested error when this magnitude is at most 0.1, giving i^2+2i ≥ 10, option d. This assumes i denotes the final summation index; counting i terms instead would shift the indexing. No Math Academy answer evidence is captured.

Given that S=∑n=2∞(−1)nn2−1 and that si is the ith partial sum of S, use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of i such that |S−si|<0.1.

a
i2+4i≥98
b
i2+2i≥8
c
i2+4i≥10
d
i2+2i≥10
e
i2+2i≥100
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let an=1n2−1 and bn=(−1)nn2−1. Then an is decreasing for n≥2 and an→0 as n→∞. So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the ith partial sum, it states that |S−si|<|bi+1|.

So, we require

|bi+1|=|(−1)i+1(i+1)2−1|≤0.11i2+2i+1−1≤1101i2+2i≤110i2+2i≥10.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Given that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{2}^{n}}
$$

and that ${s}_{i}$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of $i$ such that $|S-{s}_{i}|<0.01.$
question.worked_solution:
First, let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{2}^{n}}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{2}^{n}}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing for $n\ge 1$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test. 

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{i}|<|{b}_{i+1}|.
$$

So, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}|{b}_{i+1}|=|\frac{(-1)^{i+1}}{{2}^{i+1}}| & \le 0.01 \\ \frac{1}{{2}^{i+1}} & \le \frac{1}{100} \\ 100 & \le {2}^{i+1} \\ 100 & \le 2\cdot {2}^{i} \\ {2}^{i} & \ge 50.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Given that S=∑n=1∞(−1)n2n and that si is the ith partial sum of S, use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of i such that |S−si|<0.01.

a
2i≥52
b
2i≥100
c
2i≥48
d
2i≥98
e
2i≥50
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let an=12n and bn=(−1)n2n. Then an is decreasing for n≥1 and an→0 as n→∞. So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the ith partial sum, it states that |S−si|<|bi+1|.

So, we require |bi+1|=|(−1)i+12i+1|≤0.0112i+1≤1100100≤2i+1100≤2⋅2i2i≥50.

solution.reasoning: The first omitted term has magnitude 1/2^{i+1}. Requiring this bound to be at most 0.01 gives 2^{i+1} ≥ 100, hence 2^i ≥ 50 (option e). For integer i this means i ≥ 6, and the error is strictly below 0.01. No captured Math Academy answer evidence establishes its key.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Given that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{2}^{n}}
$$

and that ${s}_{i}$ is the $i$th partial sum of $S,$ use the alternating series error bound to determine an inequality that gives the values of $i$ such that $|S-{s}_{i}|<0.01.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{2}^{n}}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{2}^{n}}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing for $n\ge 1$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test. 

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $i$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{i}|<|{b}_{i+1}|.
$$

So, we require

$$
\begin{aligned}|{b}_{i+1}|=|\frac{(-1)^{i+1}}{{2}^{i+1}}| & \le 0.01 \\ \frac{1}{{2}^{i+1}} & \le \frac{1}{100} \\ 100 & \le {2}^{i+1} \\ 100 & \le 2\cdot {2}^{i} \\ {2}^{i} & \ge 50.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Suppose that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{(-1)}^{n}}{{e}^{n+2}}
$$

and that ${s}_{6}$ is the sixth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-{s}_{6}|<k$ for some real number $k.$

Find the value of $k.$ Do not round the answer.

$k=$

{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=\frac{1}{{e}^{n+2}}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{e}^{n+2}}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is positive and decreasing for $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $6$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{6}|<|{b}_{7}|=|\frac{{(-1)}^{7}}{{e}^{7+2}}|=\frac{1}{{e}^{9}}.
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{1}{{e}^{9}}.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Suppose that

$$
S={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{(-2)}^{n}}{(n+1)!}
$$

and that ${s}_{5}$ is the fifth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-{s}_{5}|<k$ for some real number $k.$ Find the value of $k.$ Do not round the answer.

$k=$

{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=\frac{{2}^{n}}{(n+1)!}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{{(-2)}^{n}}{(n+1)!}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is positive and decreasing for $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $5$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{5}|<|{b}_{6}|=|\frac{{(-2)}^{6}}{(6+1)!}|=\frac{64}{5040}=\frac{4}{315}.
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{4}{315}.$

and that ${s}_{5}$ is the fifth partial sum of $S.$ According to the alternating series error bound, $|S-{s}_{5}|<k$ for some real number $k.$ Find the value of $k.$ Do not round the answer.

$k=$

{{field-1}}
feedback.worked_solution:
Let ${a}_{n}=\frac{{2}^{n}}{(n+1)!}$ and ${b}_{n}=\frac{{(-2)}^{n}}{(n+1)!}.$ Then ${a}_{n}$ is positive and decreasing for $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, the series is convergent by the alternating series test.

Because our series is a convergent alternating series, the alternating series error bound applies. In particular, for the $5$th partial sum, it states that

$$
|S-{s}_{5}|<|{b}_{6}|=|\frac{{(-2)}^{6}}{(6+1)!}|=\frac{64}{5040}=\frac{4}{315}.
$$

Therefore, $k=\frac{4}{315}.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Express ${log}_{5}⁡2+{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡6$ as a single logarithm.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms, we can combine the first two terms as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡2+{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡6 & ={log}_{5}⁡(2\cdot 4)+{log}_{5}⁡6 \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡8+{log}_{5}⁡6\end{aligned}
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms once more, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡8+{log}_{5}⁡6 & ={log}_{5}⁡(8\cdot 6) \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡48.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Write the following expression as a single logarithm.

$5\operatorname{ln}⁡p+5\operatorname{ln}⁡q+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(pq)=5\operatorname{ln}⁡(${{field-1}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{ln}⁡p+5\operatorname{ln}⁡q+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(pq) & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡p+\operatorname{ln}⁡q+\operatorname{ln}⁡(pq)) \\  & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(p\cdot q\cdot pq) \\  & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡({p}^{2}{q}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)

$$
8\operatorname{ln}⁡7+8\operatorname{ln}⁡3=8\operatorname{ln}⁡21.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Express $4\operatorname{log}⁡2+4\operatorname{log}⁡4+4\operatorname{log}⁡8$ as a single logarithm.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{log}⁡2+4\operatorname{log}⁡4+4\operatorname{log}⁡8 & =4(\operatorname{log}⁡2+4\operatorname{log}⁡4+\operatorname{log}⁡8) \\  & =4\operatorname{log}⁡(2\cdot 4\cdot 8) \\  & =4\operatorname{log}⁡64.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
4\operatorname{log}⁡2+4\operatorname{log}⁡4+4\operatorname{log}⁡8=4\operatorname{log}⁡64.
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Write the following expression as a single logarithm.

$4\operatorname{log}⁡t+4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{2})+4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{3})=4\operatorname{log}⁡(${{field-1}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{log}⁡t+4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{2})+4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{3}) & =4(\operatorname{log}⁡t+\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{2})+\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{3})) \\  & =4\operatorname{log}⁡(t\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot {t}^{3}) \\  & =4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{1+2+3}) \\  & =4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{6}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Express $5{log}_{3}⁡4+5{log}_{3}⁡5$ as a single logarithm.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5{log}_{3}⁡4+5{log}_{3}⁡5 & =5({log}_{3}⁡4+{log}_{3}⁡5) \\  & =5{log}_{3}⁡(4\cdot 5) \\  & =5{log}_{3}⁡20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
5{log}_{3}⁡4+5{log}_{3}⁡5=5{log}_{3}⁡20.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}9\operatorname{log}⁡(6z) & =9(\operatorname{log}⁡6+\operatorname{log}⁡z) \\  & =9\operatorname{log}⁡6+9\operatorname{log}⁡z.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: $\operatorname{log}⁡(100{x}^{2})=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡(100{x}^{2})=\operatorname{log}⁡100+\operatorname{log}⁡({x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $100={10}^{2},$ we have

$$
\operatorname{log}⁡100=\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{2})=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡(100{x}^{2}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡100+\operatorname{log}⁡({x}^{2}) \\  & =2+\operatorname{log}⁡({x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Combining Logarithms Using the Product Rule
canonical_examples.problem: Express $\log_3(2)+\log_3(5)$ as a single logarithm.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n a + \log_n b = \log_n(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{3}⁡2+{log}_{3}⁡5 & ={log}_{3}⁡(2\cdot 5) \\  & ={log}_{3}⁡10.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Combining Logarithms With Coefficients Using the Product Rule
canonical_examples.problem: Express $3\log_{5}{7}+3\log_{5}{3}$ as a single logarithm.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n a + \log_n b = \log_n(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{log}_{5}⁡7+3{log}_{5}⁡3 & =3({log}_{5}⁡7+{log}_{5}⁡3) \\  & =3{log}_{5}⁡(7\cdot 3) \\  & =3{log}_{5}⁡21.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
3\log_{5}{7}+3\log_{5}{3} = 3\log_{5} 21 .
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Separating a Logarithm Into Two Logarithms Using the Product Rule
canonical_examples.problem: Express $\ln\left(x^2 y\right)$ as a sum of two logarithms.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for natural logarithms:

$$
\ln{a} + \ln{b} = \ln(ab)
$$

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}y) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}\cdot y) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: If $\log_2(3)=k$ and $\log_2(x)=p,$ what is the value of $\log_2(3x)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
\log_n a + \log_n b = \log_n(ab)
$$

Using the product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(3x) & ={log}_{2}⁡3+{log}_{2}⁡x \\  & =k+p.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We can simplify the addition of two logarithms that share a base using the **product rule** for logarithms.

The **product rule** states that two logarithms which share a common base $\color{blue}n$ satisfy

$$
\log_{\color{blue}n}(a) + \log_{\color{blue}n}(b) = \log_{\color{blue}n}\left( ab\right).
$$

So, we can use the product rule to rewrite $\log_{\color{blue}5}(4) + \log_{\color{blue}5}(3)$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡(3) & ={log}_{5}⁡(4\cdot 3) \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡(12).\end{aligned}
$$

The product rule works exactly the same for the natural and common logarithms.

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

question.html:
Question 7
?

Express 5log3⁡4+5log3⁡5 as a single logarithm.

a
10log3⁡20
b
10log3⁡9
c
5log3⁡20
d
5log6⁡9
e
5log6⁡20
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

5log3⁡4+5log3⁡5=5(log3⁡4+log3⁡5)=5log3⁡(4⋅5)=5log3⁡20.

Therefore, 5log3⁡4+5log3⁡5=5log3⁡20.

\ln{a} + \ln{b} = \ln(ab)
$$

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}y) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}\cdot y) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

a
log⁡2+log⁡(x2)

e
2+log⁡(x2)

EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as log⁡(100x2)=log⁡100+log⁡(x2).

Since 100=102, we have log⁡100=log⁡(102)=2.

Therefore, log⁡(100x2)=log⁡100+log⁡(x2)=2+log⁡(x2).

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Express ${log}_{5}⁡2+{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡6$ as a single logarithm.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms, we can combine the first two terms as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡2+{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡6 & ={log}_{5}⁡(2\cdot 4)+{log}_{5}⁡6 \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡8+{log}_{5}⁡6\end{aligned}
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms once more, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡8+{log}_{5}⁡6 & ={log}_{5}⁡(8\cdot 6) \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡48.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Combining Logarithms Using the Product Rule
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms, we can combine the first two terms as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡2+{log}_{5}⁡4+{log}_{5}⁡6 & ={log}_{5}⁡(2\cdot 4)+{log}_{5}⁡6 \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡8+{log}_{5}⁡6\end{aligned}
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms once more, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{5}⁡8+{log}_{5}⁡6 & ={log}_{5}⁡(8\cdot 6) \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡48.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Express log5⁡2+log5⁡4+log5⁡6 as a single logarithm.

a
log5⁡10
b
log125⁡48
c
log15⁡48
d
log15⁡12
e
log5⁡48
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule for logarithms, we can combine the first two terms as follows: log5⁡2+log5⁡4+log5⁡6=log5⁡(2⋅4)+log5⁡6=log5⁡8+log5⁡6

Using the product rule for logarithms once more, we obtain log5⁡8+log5⁡6=log5⁡(8⋅6)=log5⁡48.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Express ${log}_{6}⁡8+{log}_{6}⁡3+{log}_{6}⁡2$ as a single logarithm.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms, we can combine the first two terms as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{6}⁡8+{log}_{6}⁡3+{log}_{6}⁡2 & ={log}_{6}⁡(8\cdot 3)+{log}_{6}⁡2 \\  & ={log}_{6}⁡24+{log}_{6}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms once more, we obtain

$$

Express log6⁡8+log6⁡3+log6⁡2 as a single logarithm.

a
log6⁡13
b
log6⁡48
c
log18⁡48
d
log216⁡48
e
log18⁡13
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule for logarithms, we can combine the first two terms as follows: log6⁡8+log6⁡3+log6⁡2=log6⁡(8⋅3)+log6⁡2=log6⁡24+log6⁡2

Using the product rule for logarithms once more, we obtain log6⁡24+log6⁡2=log6⁡(24⋅2)=log6⁡48.

question.problem:

$5\operatorname{ln}⁡p+5\operatorname{ln}⁡q+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(pq)=5\operatorname{ln}⁡(${{field-1}}$)$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{ln}⁡p+5\operatorname{ln}⁡q+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(pq) & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡p+\operatorname{ln}⁡q+\operatorname{ln}⁡(pq)) \\  & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(p\cdot q\cdot pq) \\  & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡({p}^{2}{q}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Express $8\operatorname{ln}⁡7+8\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ as a single logarithm.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8\operatorname{ln}⁡7+8\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & =8(\operatorname{ln}⁡7+\operatorname{ln}⁡3) \\  & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡(7\cdot 3) \\  & =8\operatorname{ln}⁡21.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
8\operatorname{ln}⁡7+8\operatorname{ln}⁡3=8\operatorname{ln}⁡21.
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{log}⁡2+4\operatorname{log}⁡4+4\operatorname{log}⁡8 & =4(\operatorname{log}⁡2+4\operatorname{log}⁡4+\operatorname{log}⁡8) \\  & =4\operatorname{log}⁡(2\cdot 4\cdot 8) \\  & =4\operatorname{log}⁡64.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
4\operatorname{log}⁡2+4\operatorname{log}⁡4+4\operatorname{log}⁡8=4\operatorname{log}⁡64.
$$

question.problem:
Write the following expression as a single logarithm.

$4\operatorname{log}⁡t+4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{2})+4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{3})=4\operatorname{log}⁡(${{field-1}}$)$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{log}⁡t+4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{2})+4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{3}) & =4(\operatorname{log}⁡t+\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{2})+\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{3})) \\  & =4\operatorname{log}⁡(t\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot {t}^{3}) \\  & =4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{1+2+3}) \\  & =4\operatorname{log}⁡({t}^{6}).\end{aligned}
$$

5log6⁡20

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Therefore, 5log3⁡4+5log3⁡5=5log3⁡20.

question.html:
Question 7
?

Express 5log3⁡4+5log3⁡5 as a single logarithm.

a
10log3⁡20
b
10log3⁡9
c
5log3⁡20
d
5log6⁡9
e
5log6⁡20
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

5log3⁡4+5log3⁡5=5(log3⁡4+log3⁡5)=5log3⁡(4⋅5)=5log3⁡20.

Therefore, 5log3⁡4+5log3⁡5=5log3⁡20.

solution.reasoning: Factoring out 5 and applying the product rule gives 5(\log_3 4+\log_3 5)=5\log_3(4\cdot5)=5\log_3 20, so option c is mathematically correct. This also equals \log_3(20^5). No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: Express $5{log}_{3}⁡4+5{log}_{3}⁡5$ as a single logarithm.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

If we factor the given expression and use the product rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5{log}_{3}⁡4+5{log}_{3}⁡5 & =5({log}_{3}⁡4+{log}_{3}⁡5) \\  & =5{log}_{3}⁡(4\cdot 5) \\  & =5{log}_{3}⁡20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
5{log}_{3}⁡4+5{log}_{3}⁡5=5{log}_{3}⁡20.
$$

Question 8
?

6log2⁡(x2y)=

a
6log2⁡(x2)+log2⁡y
b
6log2⁡(x2)+6log2⁡y
c
log2⁡(6x2)⋅log2⁡y
d
6log2⁡(x2)⋅log2⁡y
e
log2⁡(6x2)+log2⁡y
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule for logarithms and the distributive law, we obtain 6log2⁡(x2y)=6(log2⁡(x2)+log2⁡y)=6log2⁡(x2)+6log2⁡y.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms and the distributive law, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}6{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2}y) & =6({log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2})+{log}_{2}⁡y) \\  & =6{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2})+6{log}_{2}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

6log2⁡(x2y)=

a
6log2⁡(x2)+log2⁡y
b
6log2⁡(x2)+6log2⁡y
c
log2⁡(6x2)⋅log2⁡y
d
6log2⁡(x2)⋅log2⁡y
e
log2⁡(6x2)+log2⁡y
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule for logarithms and the distributive law, we obtain 6log2⁡(x2y)=6(log2⁡(x2)+log2⁡y)=6log2⁡(x2)+6log2⁡y.
question.knowledge_point: Separating a Logarithm Into Two Logarithms Using the Product Rule

solution.reasoning: For x≠0 and y>0, the product rule gives 6\log_2(x^2y)=6(\log_2(x^2)+\log_2 y)=6\log_2(x^2)+6\log_2 y. Thus option b is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms and the distributive law, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}6{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2}y) & =6({log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2})+{log}_{2}⁡y) \\  & =6{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2})+6{log}_{2}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: $9\operatorname{log}⁡(6z)=$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms and the distributive law, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9\operatorname{log}⁡(6z) & =9(\operatorname{log}⁡6+\operatorname{log}⁡z) \\  & =9\operatorname{log}⁡6+9\operatorname{log}⁡z.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 9
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Separating a Logarithm Into Two Logarithms Using the Product Rule
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule for logarithms and the distributive law, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}9\operatorname{log}⁡(6z) & =9(\operatorname{log}⁡6+\operatorname{log}⁡z) \\  & =9\operatorname{log}⁡6+9\operatorname{log}⁡z.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}⁡(16{x}^{3})={log}_{4}⁡16+{log}_{4}⁡({x}^{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $16={4}^{2},$ we have

$$
{log}_{4}⁡16={log}_{4}⁡({4}^{2})=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}⁡(16{x}^{3}) & ={log}_{4}⁡16+{log}_{4}⁡({x}^{3}) \\  & =2+{log}_{4}⁡({x}^{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

log4⁡(16x3)=

a
4+log4⁡(2x3)
b
2log4⁡(x3)
c
2+log4⁡(x3)
d
1+log4⁡(2x3)
e
4log4⁡(x3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as log4⁡(16x3)=log4⁡16+log4⁡(x3).

Since 16=42, we have log4⁡16=log4⁡(42)=2.

Therefore, log4⁡(16x3)=log4⁡16+log4⁡(x3)=2+log4⁡(x3).

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Separating a Logarithm Into Two Logarithms Using the Product Rule
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}⁡(16{x}^{3})={log}_{4}⁡16+{log}_{4}⁡({x}^{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $16={4}^{2},$ we have

$$
{log}_{4}⁡16={log}_{4}⁡({4}^{2})=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}⁡(16{x}^{3}) & ={log}_{4}⁡16+{log}_{4}⁡({x}^{3}) \\  & =2+{log}_{4}⁡({x}^{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

log4⁡(16x3)=

a
4+log4⁡(2x3)
b
2log4⁡(x3)
c
2+log4⁡(x3)
d
1+log4⁡(2x3)
e
4log4⁡(x3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as log4⁡(16x3)=log4⁡16+log4⁡(x3).

Since 16=42, we have log4⁡16=log4⁡(42)=2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡(100{x}^{2})=\operatorname{log}⁡100+\operatorname{log}⁡({x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $100={10}^{2},$ we have

$$
\operatorname{log}⁡100=\operatorname{log}⁡({10}^{2})=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{log}⁡(100{x}^{2}) & =\operatorname{log}⁡100+\operatorname{log}⁡({x}^{2}) \\  & =2+\operatorname{log}⁡({x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 11
?

log⁡(100x2)=

a
log⁡2+log⁡(x2)
b
4+log⁡x
c
10+log⁡(x2)
d
20+log⁡x
e
2+log⁡(x2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as log⁡(100x2)=log⁡100+log⁡(x2).

Since 100=102, we have log⁡100=log⁡(102)=2.

Therefore, log⁡(100x2)=log⁡100+log⁡(x2)=2+log⁡(x2).

a
log⁡2+log⁡(x2)
b
4+log⁡x
c
10+log⁡(x2)
d
20+log⁡x
e
2+log⁡(x2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as log⁡(100x2)=log⁡100+log⁡(x2).

Since 100=102, we have log⁡100=log⁡(102)=2.

Therefore, log⁡(100x2)=log⁡100+log⁡(x2)=2+log⁡(x2).

question.name: Question 12
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
{log}_{2}⁡(32{x}^{2})={log}_{2}⁡32+{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2}).
$$

Since $32={2}^{5},$ we have

$$
{log}_{2}⁡32={log}_{2}⁡({2}^{5})=5.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(32{x}^{2}) & ={log}_{2}⁡32+{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2}) \\  & =5+{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Separating a Logarithm Into Two Logarithms Using the Product Rule
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

$$
{log}_{n}⁡a+{log}_{n}⁡b={log}_{n}⁡(ab)
$$

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as

$$
{log}_{2}⁡(32{x}^{2})={log}_{2}⁡32+{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2}).
$$

Since $32={2}^{5},$ we have

$$
{log}_{2}⁡32={log}_{2}⁡({2}^{5})=5.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(32{x}^{2}) & ={log}_{2}⁡32+{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2}) \\  & =5+{log}_{2}⁡({x}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 12
?

log2⁡(32x2)=

a
log2⁡(5x2)
b
5+log2⁡(x2)
c
3+log2⁡(x2)
d
5log2⁡(x2)
e
3+log2⁡(2x2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule, the given expression can be rewritten as log2⁡(32x2)=log2⁡32+log2⁡(x2).

Since 32=25, we have log2⁡32=log2⁡(25)=5.

Therefore, log2⁡(32x2)=log2⁡32+log2⁡(x2)=5+log2⁡(x2).

question.html:
Question 14
?

If ln⁡x=10 and ln⁡y=2, then ln⁡(xy)=

a
10x+2y
b
12
c
x10y2
d
20xy
e
20
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the product rule for logarithms:

logn⁡a+logn⁡b=logn⁡(ab)

Using the product rule, we have

ln⁡(xy)=ln⁡x+ln⁡y=10+2=12.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
In a store, there are three different types of cream cheese that come in boxes: 

- Box $A$ contains $1$ cup and costs $$1.96\,.$

- Box $B$ contains $1.2$ cups and costs $$2.40\,.$

- Box $C$ contains $1.5$ cups and costs $$2.94\,.$

Which box of cream cheese is the best deal?
questions.worked_solution:
The best deal is the one with the lowest unit price. So, we need to compute the unit prices for all three boxes. To compute the unit price, we divide the price by the total number of cups.   

- Dividing the total cost by the number of cups in box $A,$ we get

$$
1.96÷1=1.96\,.
$$

So, the unit price of box $A$ is $$1.96.$

- Dividing the total cost by the number of cups in box $B,$ we get

$$
2.40÷1.2=2\,.
$$

So, the unit price of box $B$ is $$2.00.$

- Dividing the total cost by the number of cups in box $C,$ we get

$$
2.94÷1.5=1.96\,.
$$

So, the unit price of box $C$ is $$1.96$  too.

From the above, we see that boxes $A$ and $C$  have the lowest unit price. Therefore, boxes $A$ and  $C$ are the best deal.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Nathan, a freelance journalist, charges $$0.04$ per word for his financial articles. How many words would it take for him to earn $1$ dollar?
questions.worked_solution:
We are given the unit rate of $$0.04$ per word (dollars per word). To find how many words  it would take for him to earn $1$ dollar we need to find the unit rate in words per dollar. So, we take the reciprocal: 

$$
0.04\,\text{dollars per word}\,\to \,1÷0.04=25\,\text{words per dollar}
$$

So, the unit rate is $25$ words per dollar. Therefore, Nathan writes $25$ words for $1$ dollar.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Louis visits a snack shop, the unit price for nuts is $$8$ per pound. How many pounds of nuts can Louis buy for $$1?$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given the unit rate of $$8$ per pound (dollars per pound). To find how many pounds of nuts she can buy for  $$1,$ we need to find the unit rate in pounds per dollar. So, we take the reciprocal: 

$$
8\,\text{dollars per pound}\,\to \,1÷8=0.125\,\text{pounds per dollar}
$$

So, the unit rate is $0.125$ pounds per dollar. Therefore, Louis can buy $0.125$ pounds of nuts for $1$ dollar.

$$
0.08\,\text{dollars per foot}\,\to \,1÷0.08=12.5\,\text{feet per dollar}
$$

So, the unit rate is $12.5$ feet per dollar. Therefore, Anne can buy $12.5$ feet of copper wire.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
John wonders what bottle of juice to buy from three different types available at the convenience store:

- Bottle $A$ contains $20$ ounces, and costs $$3.00\,.$

- Bottle $B$ contains $32$ ounces, and costs $$4.80\,.$

- Bottle $C$ contains $10$ ounces, and costs $$1.80\,.$

Which bottle of juice is the best deal?
questions.worked_solution:
The best deal is the one with the lowest unit price. So, we need to compute the unit prices for all three bottles. To compute the unit price, we divide the cost by the total number of ounces.

- Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in bottle $A$,  we get

$$
3.00÷20=0.15\,.
$$

So, the unit price of bottle $A$ is $$0.15$  per ounce.

- Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in bottle $B$,  we get

$$
4.80÷32=0.15\,.
$$

So, the unit price of bottle $B$ is $$0.15$  per ounce.

- Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in bottle $C$,  we get

$$
1.80÷10=0.18\,.
$$

So, the unit price of bottle $C$ is $$0.18$  per ounce.

From the above, we see that bottles $A$ and $B$ have the lowest unit price. Therefore, bottles $A$ and $B$ are the best deal.

question.html:
Question 1
?

In a store, there are three different types of cream cheese that come in boxes:

  • Box A contains 1 cup and costs $1.96.

  • Box B contains 1.2 cups and costs $2.40.

  • Box C contains 1.5 cups and costs $2.94.

Which box of cream cheese is the best deal?

a
A only
b
A and B only
c
B only
d
A and C only
e
B and C only
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The best deal is the one with the lowest unit price. So, we need to compute the unit prices for all three boxes. To compute the unit price, we divide the price by the total number of cups.

  • Dividing the total cost by the number of cups in box A, we get 1.96÷1=1.96. So, the unit price of box A is $1.96.

  • Dividing the total cost by the number of cups in box B, we get 2.40÷1.2=2. So, the unit price of box B is $2.00.

  • Dividing the total cost by the number of cups in box C, we get 2.94÷1.5=1.96. So, the unit price of box C is $1.96 too.

From the above, we see that boxes A and C have the lowest unit price. Therefore, boxes A and C are the best deal.

Question 1
?

In a store, there are three different types of cream cheese that come in boxes:

  • Box A contains 1 cup and costs $1.96.

  • Box B contains 1.2 cups and costs $2.40.

  • Box C contains 1.5 cups and costs $2.94.

Which box of cream cheese is the best deal?

a
A only
b
A and B only
c
B only
d
A and C only
e
B and C only
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The best deal is the one with the lowest unit price. So, we need to compute the unit prices for all three boxes. To compute the unit price, we divide the price by the total number of cups.

  • Dividing the total cost by the number of cups in box A, we get 1.96÷1=1.96. So, the unit price of box A is $1.96.

  • Dividing the total cost by the number of cups in box B, we get 2.40÷1.2=2. So, the unit price of box B is $2.00.

  • Dividing the total cost by the number of cups in box C, we get 2.94÷1.5=1.96. So, the unit price of box C is $1.96 too.

From the above, we see that boxes A and C have the lowest unit price. Therefore, boxes A and C are the best deal.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Nathan, a freelance journalist, charges $$0.04$ per word for his financial articles. How many words would it take for him to earn $1$ dollar?
question.worked_solution:
We are given the unit rate of $$0.04$ per word (dollars per word). To find how many words  it would take for him to earn $1$ dollar we need to find the unit rate in words per dollar. So, we take the reciprocal: 

$$
0.04\,\text{dollars per word}\,\to \,1÷0.04=25\,\text{words per dollar}
$$

So, the unit rate is $25$ words per dollar. Therefore, Nathan writes $25$ words for $1$ dollar.

question.html:
Question 4
?

Anne needs to buy copper wire, the unit price for the copper wire is $0.08 per foot. How many feet of cooper wire can Anne buy with $1?

a
8.7 feet
b
10.9 feet
c
10.5 feet
d
12.5 feet
e
11.4 feet
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We are given the unit rate of $0.08 per foot (dollars per foot). To find the amount of copper wire that Anne can buy for $1, we need to find the unit rate in feet per dollar. So, we take the reciprocal:

0.08dollars per foot→1÷0.08=12.5feet per dollar

So, the unit rate is 12.5 feet per dollar. Therefore, Anne can buy 12.5 feet of copper wire.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
John wonders what bottle of juice to buy from three different types available at the convenience store:

- Bottle $A$ contains $20$ ounces, and costs $$3.00\,.$

- Bottle $B$ contains $32$ ounces, and costs $$4.80\,.$

- Bottle $C$ contains $10$ ounces, and costs $$1.80\,.$

Which bottle of juice is the best deal?
question.worked_solution:
The best deal is the one with the lowest unit price. So, we need to compute the unit prices for all three bottles. To compute the unit price, we divide the cost by the total number of ounces.

- Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in bottle $A$,  we get

$$
3.00÷20=0.15\,.
$$

So, the unit price of bottle $A$ is $$0.15$  per ounce.

- Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in bottle $B$,  we get

$$
4.80÷32=0.15\,.
$$

So, the unit price of bottle $B$ is $$0.15$  per ounce.

- Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in bottle $C$,  we get

$$
1.80÷10=0.18\,.
$$

So, the unit price of bottle $C$ is $$0.18$  per ounce.

From the above, we see that bottles $A$ and $B$ have the lowest unit price. Therefore, bottles $A$ and $B$ are the best deal.

  • Bottle B contains 32 ounces, and costs $4.80.

  • Bottle C contains 10 ounces, and costs $1.80.

Which bottle of juice is the best deal?

a
C only
b
A and B only
c
A only
d
B only
e
A and C only
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The best deal is the one with the lowest unit price. So, we need to compute the unit prices for all three bottles. To compute the unit price, we divide the cost by the total number of ounces.

  • Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in bottle A, we get 3.00÷20=0.15. So, the unit price of bottle A is $0.15 per ounce.

  • Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in bottle B, we get 4.80÷32=0.15. So, the unit price of bottle B is $0.15 per ounce.

  • Dividing the total cost by the number of ounces in bottle C, we get 1.80÷10=0.18. So, the unit price of bottle C is $0.18 per ounce.

From the above, we see that bottles A and B have the lowest unit price. Therefore, bottles A and B are the best deal.

solution.reasoning: The prices per ounce are A: 3.00/20 = $0.15, B: 4.80/32 = $0.15, and C: 1.80/10 = $0.18. A and B tie for the lowest price per ounce, so option b is correct mathematically. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: $\int (-\operatorname{sech}⁡t\operatorname{tanh}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sech}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sech}⁡t\operatorname{tanh}⁡t\,⇒\,\int \operatorname{sech}⁡t\operatorname{tanh}⁡t\,\text{d}t=-\operatorname{sech}⁡t+C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-\operatorname{sech}⁡t\operatorname{tanh}⁡t)\,\text{d}t & =-\int \operatorname{sech}⁡t\operatorname{tanh}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-(-\operatorname{sech}⁡t)+C \\  & =\operatorname{sech}⁡t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: $\int (5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y)\text{d}y=$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡y)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{csch}⁡y)=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y)\text{d}y & =\int 5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+\int 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+3\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5(-\operatorname{csch}⁡y)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C \\  & =3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y-5\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int (-{sech}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡t)={sech}^{2}⁡t\,⇒\,\int {sech}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{tanh}⁡t+C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-{sech}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t & =-\int {sech}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\operatorname{tanh}⁡t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int (4-3{sech}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta =$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{tanh}⁡\theta )={sech}^{2}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\int {sech}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =\operatorname{tanh}⁡\theta +C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4-3{sech}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & =\int 4\,\text{d}\theta +\int (-3{sech}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\int \,\text{d}\theta -3\int {sech}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\theta -3\operatorname{tanh}⁡\theta +C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int ({csch}^{2}⁡x-4{sech}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x)={sech}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)=-{csch}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{coth}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({csch}^{2}⁡x-4{sech}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x-4\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{coth}⁡x-4\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡y)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{csch}⁡y)=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y)\text{d}y & =\int 5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+\int 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+3\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5(-\operatorname{csch}⁡y)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C \\  & =3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y-5\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

∫(csch2⁡x−4sech2⁡x)dx=∫csch2⁡xdx−4∫sech2⁡xdx=−coth⁡x−4tanh⁡x+C.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: $\int (-\operatorname{sech}⁡t\operatorname{tanh}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sech}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sech}⁡t\operatorname{tanh}⁡t\,⇒\,\int \operatorname{sech}⁡t\operatorname{tanh}⁡t\,\text{d}t=-\operatorname{sech}⁡t+C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-\operatorname{sech}⁡t\operatorname{tanh}⁡t)\,\text{d}t & =-\int \operatorname{sech}⁡t\operatorname{tanh}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-(-\operatorname{sech}⁡t)+C \\  & =\operatorname{sech}⁡t+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: $\int (5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y)\text{d}y=$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡y)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{csch}⁡y)=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y)\text{d}y & =\int 5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+\int 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+3\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5(-\operatorname{csch}⁡y)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C \\  & =3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y-5\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡y)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{csch}⁡y)=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y)\text{d}y & =\int 5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+\int 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+3\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5(-\operatorname{csch}⁡y)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C \\  & =3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y-5\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: $\int (5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y)\text{d}y=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sinh}⁡y)=\operatorname{cosh}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{csch}⁡y)=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y & \,⇒\,\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y=-\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y+3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y)\text{d}y & =\int 5\operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+\int 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csch}⁡y\operatorname{coth}⁡y\,\text{d}y+3\int \operatorname{cosh}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =5(-\operatorname{csch}⁡y)+3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y+C \\  & =3\operatorname{sinh}⁡y-5\operatorname{csch}⁡y+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: $\int (-{sech}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t=$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡t)={sech}^{2}⁡t\,⇒\,\int {sech}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{tanh}⁡t+C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{tanh}⁡\theta )={sech}^{2}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\int {sech}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =\operatorname{tanh}⁡\theta +C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4-3{sech}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & =\int 4\,\text{d}\theta +\int (-3{sech}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\int \,\text{d}\theta -3\int {sech}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\theta -3\operatorname{tanh}⁡\theta +C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: $\int ({csch}^{2}⁡x-4{sech}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x)={sech}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)=-{csch}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{coth}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({csch}^{2}⁡x-4{sech}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x-4\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{coth}⁡x-4\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x)={sech}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)=-{csch}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{coth}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({csch}^{2}⁡x-4{sech}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x-4\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{coth}⁡x-4\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

∫(csch2⁡x−4sech2⁡x)dx=

a
coth⁡x+4tanh⁡x+C
b
coth2⁡x−4tanh⁡x+C
c
−coth⁡x−4tanh⁡x+C
d
coth⁡x−4tanh⁡x+C
e
−coth2⁡x+4tanh⁡x+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that ddx(tanh⁡x)=sech2⁡x⇒∫sech2⁡xdx=tanh⁡x+C,ddx(coth⁡x)=−csch2⁡x⇒∫csch2⁡xdx=−coth⁡x+C.

Therefore, we have

∫(csch2⁡x−4sech2⁡x)dx=∫csch2⁡xdx−4∫sech2⁡xdx=−coth⁡x−4tanh⁡x+C.

solution.reasoning: Since (coth x)' = −csch² x and (tanh x)' = sech² x, the integral is −coth x − 4 tanh x + C, choice c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: $\int ({csch}^{2}⁡x-4{sech}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{tanh}⁡x)={sech}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C, \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{coth}⁡x)=-{csch}^{2}⁡x & \,⇒\,\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{coth}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({csch}^{2}⁡x-4{sech}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int {csch}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x-4\int {sech}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{coth}⁡x-4\operatorname{tanh}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=-2{x}^{2}+10x-3$ is $x=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is given by

questions.problem: Find the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola $y=-2{x}^{2}+4x-9.$
questions.worked_solution:
The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry. 

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}.
$$

Substituting $a=-2$ and $b=4$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{4}{2(-2)} \\  & =-\frac{4}{(-4)} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=1.$ This also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute $x=1$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2{x}^{2}+4x-9 \\  & =-2(1)^{2}+4(1)-9 \\  & =-2+4-9 \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(1,-7).$

questions.problem: Find the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola $y=-4{x}^{2}-24x-10.$
questions.worked_solution:
The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry. 

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}.
$$

Substituting $a=-4$ and $b=-24$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{(-24)}{2(-4)} \\  & =-\frac{(-24)}{(-8)} \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=-3.$ This also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute $x=-3$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4{x}^{2}-24x-10 \\  & =-4(-3)^{2}-24(-3)-10 \\  & =-36+72-10 \\  & =26\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(-3,26).$

x = -\dfrac{b}{2a}.

$$

We already know that the axis of symmetry is $x=-6,$ so we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2k & =-6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To determine the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=ax^2+bx+c,$ we can use the following formula:

$$
x=-\dfrac{b}{2a}
$$

We'll derive this result in a separate lesson. For now, let's get some practice working with it. 

Suppose we want to find the axis of symmetry of the function $y=3x^2-6x+1.$ To do this, we substitute $a=3$ and $b=-6$ into the above formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{b}{2a} \\  & =-\frac{(-6)}{2(3)} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=1$ is the equation of the axis of symmetry. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14224554/assets/88ee917eb387ee60e67080785519ffe9cb4333adcd602a733659d0447c37f61a.png)

The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so $x=1$ also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we can substitute $x=1$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3{x}^{2}-6x+1 \\  & =3(1)^{2}-6(1)+1 \\  & =3-6+1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(1,-2).$

Question 3
?

Find the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola y=3x2−18x−3.

a
(3,−10)
b
(−3,−30)
c
(3,−30)
d
(−2,−18)
e
(2,−27)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry.

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola y=ax2+bx+c is given by

x=−b2a.

Substituting a=3 and b=−18 into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get x=−(−18)2(3)=−(−18)6=3.

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is x=3. This also represents the x-coordinate of the vertex. To find the y-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute x=3 into the original equation: y=3x2−18x−3=3(3)2−18(3)−3=27−54−3=−30

Therefore, the vertex is at (3,−30).

The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry. 

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}.
$$

Substituting $a=3$ and $b=-18$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{(-18)}{2(3)} \\  & =-\frac{(-18)}{6} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=3.$ This also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute $x=3$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =3{x}^{2}-18x-3 \\  & =3(3)^{2}-18(3)-3 \\  & =27-54-3 \\  & =-30\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(3,-30).$

Question 3

Find the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola y=3x2−18x−3.

a
(3,−10)
b
(−3,−30)
c
(3,−30)
d
(−2,−18)
e
(2,−27)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry.

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola y=ax2+bx+c is given by

x=−b2a.

Substituting a=3 and b=−18 into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get x=−(−18)2(3)=−(−18)6=3.

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is x=3. This also represents the x-coordinate of the vertex. To find the y-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute x=3 into the original equation: y=3x2−18x−3=3(3)2−18(3)−3=27−54−3=−30

Therefore, the vertex is at (3,−30).

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Find the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola $y=-2{x}^{2}+4x-9.$
question.worked_solution:
The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry. 

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}.
$$

Substituting $a=-2$ and $b=4$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{4}{2(-2)} \\  & =-\frac{4}{(-4)} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=1.$ This also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute $x=1$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2{x}^{2}+4x-9 \\  & =-2(1)^{2}+4(1)-9 \\  & =-2+4-9 \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(1,-7).$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Find the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola y=−2x2+4x−9.

a
(2,−9)
b
(1,−7)
c
(−1,7)
d
(1,−15)
e
(−1,−15)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry.

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola y=ax2+bx+c is given by

x=−b2a.

Substituting a=−2 and b=4 into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get x=−42(−2)=−4(−4)=1.

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is x=1. This also represents the x-coordinate of the vertex. To find the y-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute x=1 into the original equation: y=−2x2+4x−9=−2(1)2+4(1)−9=−2+4−9=−7

Therefore, the vertex is at (1,−7).

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Find the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola $y=-2{x}^{2}+4x-9.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry. 

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}.
$$

Substituting $a=-2$ and $b=4$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{4}{2(-2)} \\  & =-\frac{4}{(-4)} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=1.$ This also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute $x=1$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-2{x}^{2}+4x-9 \\  & =-2(1)^{2}+4(1)-9 \\  & =-2+4-9 \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(1,-7).$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Vertex of a Parabola
last_observation.worked_solution:
The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry. 

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}.
$$

Substituting $a=-4$ and $b=-24$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-\frac{(-24)}{2(-4)} \\  & =-\frac{(-24)}{(-8)} \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is $x=-3.$ This also represents the $x$-coordinate of the vertex. To find the $y$-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute $x=-3$ into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4{x}^{2}-24x-10 \\  & =-4(-3)^{2}-24(-3)-10 \\  & =-36+72-10 \\  & =26\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertex is at $(-3,26).$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Find the coordinates of the vertex of the parabola y=−4x2−24x−10.

a
(−6,−10)
b
(3,−118)
c
(−3,−118)
d
(3,26)
e
(−3,26)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vertex of the parabola lies on the axis of symmetry, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry.

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola y=ax2+bx+c is given by

x=−b2a.

Substituting a=−4 and b=−24 into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get x=−(−24)2(−4)=−(−24)(−8)=−3.

Therefore, the equation of the axis of symmetry is x=−3. This also represents the x-coordinate of the vertex. To find the y-coordinate of the vertex, we substitute x=−3 into the original equation: y=−4x2−24x−10=−4(−3)2−24(−3)−10=−36+72−10=26

Therefore, the vertex is at (−3,26).

question.worked_solution:
The parabola's vertex lies on the symmetry axis, so we will start by computing the axis of symmetry. 

The equation of the axis of symmetry of the parabola $y=a{x}^{2}+bx+c$ is given by

$$
x=-\frac{b}{2a}.
$$

Substituting $a=-1$ and $b=-4$ into the formula for the axis of symmetry, we get

$$
